For when the audience has been made receptive through the subordinate elements of <s>��ṛṅgāra rasa</s>, they readily absorb the instruction in good conduct. For the performance of dramas and the like has been introduced by the sages for the benefit of the audience, in the form of instruction in proper conduct. Moreover, since <s>śṛṅgāra</s> is universally captivating and delightful to the minds of all, the inclusion of its subordinate elements in poetry enhances the beauty exceedingly — thus, in this way too, the inclusion of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> as a subordinate element alongside an incompatible <s>rasa</s> is not contradictory. And therefore:

children.text: satyaṃ manoramā rāmāḥ satyaṃ ramyā vibhūtayaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Truly, women are delightful; truly, splendors are charming;

children.text: kiṃ tu mattāṅganāpāṅga-bhaṅga-lolaṃ hi jīvitam //
children.translated_text: But life is as fickle as the sidelong glance of an intoxicated woman.'

children.text: ity ādiṣu nāsti rasa-virodha-doṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: In such [verses], there is no fault of <s>rasa</s>-conflict.
[<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 3.31:]

children.text: vijñāyetthaṃ rasādīnām avirodha-virodhayoḥ /
children.translated_text: Having thus understood the domain of conflict and non-conflict among <s>rasas</s> and the like,

children.text: viṣayaṃ sukaviḥ kāvyaṃ kurvan muhyati na kvacit // DhvK_3.31 //
children.translated_text: The good poet, when composing poetry, will nowhere be confused. [End of <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 3.31]

children.text: ittham anenānantaroktena prakāreṇa rasādīnāṃ rasa-bhāva-tad-ābhāsānāṃ parasparaṃ virodhasyāvirodhasya ca viṣayaṃ vijñāya sukaviḥ kāvya-viṣaye pratibhātiśaya-yuktaḥ kāvyaṃ kurvan na kvacin muhyati / evaṃ rasādiṣu virodhāvirodha-nirūpaṇasyopayogitvaṃ pratipādya vyañjaka-vācya-vācaka-nirūpaṇasyāpi tad-viṣayasya tat pratipādyate-
children.translated_text: Thus, having understood through the method just described the domain of mutual conflict and non-conflict among <s>rasas</s>, <s>bhāvas</s>, and their semblances (<s>ābhāsas</s>), a good poet endowed with the excellence of creative intuition (<s>pratibhā</s>) in the domain of poetry does not err anywhere when composing poetry. Having thus established the usefulness of determining conflict and non-conflict with respect to <s>rasas</s> and the like, the examination of the suggestor (<s>vyañjaka</s>), the expressed (<s>vācya</s>), and the expressor (<s>vācaka</s>) regarding that very subject is now set forth—
DhvK 3.32:

children.text: vācyānāṃ vācakānāṃ ca yad aucityena yojanam /
children.translated_text: The joining with propriety of the expressed meanings and the expressors,

children.text: rasādi-viṣayeṇaitat karma mukhyaṃ mahā-kaveḥ // DhvK_3.32 //
children.translated_text: with reference to <s>rasa</s> and the like — this is the primary task of a great poet. // DhvK_3.32 //

children.text: vācyānām itivṛtta-viśeṣāṇāṃ vācakānāṃ ca tad-viṣayāṇāṃ rasādi-viṣayeṇaucityena yad yojanam etan mahākaver mukhyaṃ karma / ayam eva hi mahākaver mukhyo vyāpāro yad rasādīnām eva mukhyatayā kāvyārthīkṛtya tad-vyakty-anuguṇatvena śabdānām arthānāṃ copanibandhanam || DhvA_3.32 ||
children.translated_text: The joining with propriety, with reference to <s>rasa</s> and the like, of the expressed meanings — namely, the particular narrative events (<s>itivṛtta</s>) — and of the expressors pertaining to them: this is the primary task of a great poet. For this alone is the principal activity of a great poet — that, having made <s>rasas</s> and the like the primary purpose of poetry, he composes words and meanings in conformity with their manifestation. // DhvA_3.32 //

children.text: etac ca rasāditātparyeṇa kāvyanibandhanaṃ bharatādāvapi suprasiddham eveti pratipādayitum āha-
children.translated_text: And in order to demonstrate that this composition of poetry with <s>rasa</s> and the like as its purport is well established even in <s>Bharata</s> and others, he says—
DhvK 3.33:

children.text: rasādy-anuguṇatvena vyavahāro 'rtha-śabdayoḥ /
children.translated_text: The usage of meaning and word in conformity with <s>rasa</s> and the like —

children.text: aucityavānyastā etā vṛttayo dvividhāḥ sthitāḥ // DhvK_3.33 //
children.translated_text: those that possess propriety (<s>aucitya</s>) — these are the twofold styles (<s>vṛttis</s>) as established. // DhvK_3.33 //

children.text: vyavahāro hi vṛttir ity ucyate / tatra rasānuguṇa aucityavān vācyāśrayo yo vyavahāras tā etāḥ kaiśiky-ādyā vṛttayaḥ / vācakāśrayāś copanāgarikādyāḥ / vṛttayo hi rasādi-tātparyeṇa saṃniveśitāḥ kām api nāṭyasya kāvyasya ca chāyām āvahanti / rasādayo hi dvayor api tayor jīva-bhūtāḥ / itivṛttādi tu śarīra-bhūtam eva /
children.translated_text: For 'usage' (<s>vyavahāra</s>) is called 'style' (<s>vṛtti</s>). Therein, the usage based on the expressed meaning that possesses propriety in conformity with <s>rasa</s> — these are the styles such as <s>kaiśikī</s> and the like. And those based on the expressor are <s>upanāgarikā</s> and the like. For the styles, when arranged with <s>rasa</s> and the like as their purport, bring a certain luster to both drama (<s>nāṭya</s>) and poetry (<s>kāvya</s>). For <s>rasas</s> and the like are the life-force (<s>jīva</s>) of both of them. The narrative (<s>itivṛtta</s>) and the like, however, are merely the body.

children.text: atra kecid āhuḥ-"guṇa-guṇi-vyavahāro rasādīnām itivṛttādibhiḥ saha yuktaḥ, na tu jīva-śarīra-vyavahāraḥ / rasādi-mayaṃ hi vācyaṃ pratibhāsate na tu rasādibhiḥ pṛthag-bhūtam" iti / atrocyate-yadi rasādi-mayam eva vācyaṃ yathā gauratva-mayaṃ śarīram / evaṃ sati yathā śarīre pratibhāsamāne niyamenaiva gauratvaṃ pratibhāsate sarvasya tathā vācyena sahaiva rasādayo 'pi sahṛdayasyāsahṛdayasya ca pratibhāseran / na caivam; tathā caitat pratipāditam eva prathamoddyote /
children.translated_text: Here some say: 'The relationship of attribute and attribute-possessor (<s>guṇa-guṇi-vyavahāra</s>) is appropriate between <s>rasas</s> and the like and the narrative and the like, but not the relationship of soul and body (<s>jīva-śarīra-vyavahāra</s>). For the expressed meaning appears as constituted by <s>rasa</s> and the like, and not as separate from them.' To this we reply: If the expressed meaning were constituted by <s>rasa</s> and the like, just as the body is constituted by whiteness (<s>gauratva</s>), then — just as when the body is perceived, whiteness is necessarily perceived — so too <s>rasas</s> and the like would be perceived together with the expressed meaning by both the sensitive (<s>sahṛdaya</s>) and the insensitive reader alike. But that is not the case; and this has already been demonstrated in the first <s>uddyota</s>.

children.text: syān matam / ratnānām iva jātyatvaṃ pratipattṛ-viśeṣataḥ saṃvedyaṃ vācyānāṃ rasādi-rūpatvam iti / naivam / yato yathā jātyatvena pratibhāsamāne ratne ratna-svarūpānatiriktatvam eva tasya lakṣyate tathā rasādīnām api vibhāvānubhāvādi-rūpa-vācyāvyatiriktatvam eva lakṣyeta / na caivam; na hi vibhāvānubhāva-vyabhicāriṇa eva rasā iti kasyacid avagamaḥ / ata eva ca vibhāvādi-pratīty-avinābhāvinī rasādīnāṃ pratītir iti tat-pratītyoḥ kārya-kāraṇa-bhāvena vyavasthānāt kramo 'vaśyambhāvī / sa tu lāghavān na prakāśyate "ity alakṣya-kramā eva santo vyaṅgyā rasādayaḥ" ity uktam /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] It might be thought that, like the essential quality (<s>jātyatva</s>) of gems, which is cognizable only by a particular type of perceiver, so too the <s>rasa</s>-nature of expressed meanings [is perceivable only by the sensitive]. [Reply:] Not so. For just as in a gem perceived with its essential quality, the non-difference of that [quality] from the gem's own nature is what is observed, so too the non-difference of <s>rasas</s> and the like from the expressed meaning consisting of <s>vibhāvas</s>, <s>anubhāvas</s>, and the like would be observed. But that is not the case; for no one cognizes that the <s>rasas</s> are nothing other than the <s>vibhāvas</s>, <s>anubhāvas</s>, and <s>vyabhicārins</s> themselves. And precisely for this reason, since the cognition of <s>rasas</s> and the like invariably accompanies the cognition of <s>vibhāvas</s> and the like, and since the two cognitions are established in a cause-effect relationship, a sequence (<s>krama</s>) is necessarily entailed. But that [sequence], owing to its swiftness (<s>lāghava</s>), is not manifest — hence it was said: '<s>rasas</s> and the like, being suggested, are of imperceptible sequence (<s>alakṣya-krama</s>).'

children.text: nanu śabda eva prakaraṇādy-avacchinno vācya-vyaṅgyayoḥ samam eva pratītim upajanayatīti kiṃ tatra krama-kalpanayā / na hi śabdasya vācya-pratīti-parāmarśa eva vyañjakatve nibandhanam / tathā hi gītādi-śabdebhyo 'pi rasābhivyaktir asti / na ca teṣām antarā vācya-parāmarśaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But surely the word itself, delimited by context (<s>prakaraṇa</s>) and the like, produces the cognition of the expressed and the suggested equally and simultaneously — so what is the point of postulating a sequence? For the denotative function's contact with the expressed meaning is not the basis for its suggestive power. For even from musical sounds (<s>gīta</s>) and the like, the evocation of <s>rasa</s> exists, and yet there is no intervening contact with expressed meaning in their case.

children.text: atrāpi brūmaḥ-prakaraṇādy-avacchedena vyañjakatvaṃ śabdānām ity anumatam evaitad asmākam / kiṃ tu tad-vyañjakatvaṃ teṣāṃ kadācit svarūpa-viśeṣa-nibandhanaṃ kadācid vācaka-śakti-nibandhanam / tatra yeṣāṃ vācaka-śakti-nibandhanaṃ teṣāṃ yadi vācya-pratītim antareṇaiva svarūpa-pratītyā niṣpannaṃ tad bhaven na tarhi vācaka-śakti-nibandhanam / atha tan-nibandhanaṃ tan-niyamenaiva vācya-vācaka-bhāva-pratīty-uttara-kālatvaṃ vyaṅgya-pratīteḥ prāptam eva /
children.translated_text: To this too we reply: That words have suggestive power through delimitation by context and the like — this is acknowledged by us as well. However, that suggestive power of theirs is sometimes based on the particular nature (<s>svarūpa-viśeṣa</s>) of the word itself, and sometimes based on the denotative power (<s>vācaka-śakti</s>). With regard to those [words] whose [suggestive power] is based on the denotative power — if their [suggestive effect] were accomplished merely by the cognition of their own form, without the cognition of the expressed meaning, then it would not be based on the denotative power. But if it is based on the denotative power, then it necessarily follows that the cognition of the suggested comes after the cognition of the denotation-denoted relationship.

children.text: sa tu kramo yadi lāghavān na lakṣyate tat kiṃ kriyate / yadi ca vācya-pratītim antareṇaiva prakaraṇādy-avacchinna-śabda-mātra-sādhyā rasādi-pratītiḥ syāt tad-anavadhārita-prakaraṇānāṃ vācya-vācakabhāve ca svayam avyutpannānāṃ pratipattṝṇāṃ kāvya-mātra-śravaṇād evāsau bhavet / saha-bhāve ca vācya-pratīter anupayogaḥ, upayoge vā na sahabhāvaḥ / yeṣām api svarūpa-viśeṣa-pratīti-nimittaṃ vyañjakatvaṃ yathā gītādi-śabdānāṃ teṣām api svarūpa-pratīter vyaṅgya-pratīteś ca niyama-bhāvī kramaḥ / tat tu śabdasya kriyā-paurvāparyam ananya-sādhya-tat-phala-ghaṭanāsv āśu-bhāvinīṣu vācyenāvirodhiny abhidheyāntara-vilakṣaṇe rasādau na pratīyate /
children.translated_text: If that sequence is not perceived due to its swiftness — so what can be done about that? And if the cognition of <s>rasa</s> and the like were accomplishable merely through words delimited by context without the cognition of the expressed meaning, then even for those listeners who have not ascertained the context and who are themselves unlearned in the relationship of expression — that [cognition of <s>rasa</s>] would arise from mere hearing of the poem. And if [the expressed and suggested meanings arose] simultaneously, the cognition of the expressed meaning would be useless; or if useful, they would not be simultaneous. Even for those [words] whose suggestive power is caused by the cognition of their particular form — as in musical sounds (<s>gīta</s>) and the like — there too is an invariable sequence between the cognition of their form and the cognition of the suggested. But that [sequence], being the temporal priority of the word's action — in cases where the resultant effect, not achievable by other means, arises swiftly and is not in conflict with the expressed meaning, and where the suggested [meaning] such as <s>rasa</s> and the like is entirely different from any other expressed content — is not perceived.

children.text:
kvacit tu lakṣyata eva / yathānuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya-pratītiṣu / tatrāpi katham iti ced ucyate-artha-śakti-mūlānuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgye dhvanau tāvad abhidheyasya tat-sāmarthyākṣiptasya cārthasyābhidheyāntara-vilakṣaṇatayātyanta-vilakṣaṇe ye pratītī tayor aśakya-nihnavo nimitta-nimitti-bhāva iti sphuṭam eva tatra paurvāparyam / yathā prathamoddyote pratīyamānārtha-siddhy-artham udāhṛtāsu gāthāsu / tathā-vidhe ca viṣaye vācya-vyaṅgyayor atyanta-vilakṣaṇatvād yaiva ekasya pratītiḥ saivetarasyeti na śakyate vaktum / śabda-śakti-mūlānuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgye tu dhvanau-"gāvo vaḥ pāvanānāṃ parama-parimitāṃ prītim utpādayantu" ity ādāv artha-dvaya-pratītau śābdyām artha-dvayasyopamānopameya-bhāva-pratītir upamā-vācaka-pada-virahe saty artha-sāmarthyād ākṣipteti, tatrāpi sulakṣam abhidheya-vyaṅgyālaṅkāra-pratītyoḥ paurvāparyam /
pada-prakāśa-śabda-śakti-mūlānuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgye 'pi dhvanau viśeṣaṇa-padasyobhayārtha-sambandha-yogyasya yojakaṃ padam antareṇa yojanam aśābdam apy arthād avasthitam ity atrāpi pūrvavad abhidheya-tat-sāmarthyākṣiptālaṅkāra-mātra-pratītyoḥ susthitam eva paurvāparyam / ārthy api ca pratipattis tathāvidhe viṣaye ubhayārtha-sambandha-yogya-śabda-sāmarthya-prasāviteti śabda-śakti-mūlā kalpyate /
children.translated_text: But in some cases, it is indeed perceptible — as in the cognitions of the suggested of the reverberation (<s>anuranana</s>) type. How so in those cases? To explain: In <s>dhvani</s> of the reverberation type rooted in the power of meaning (<s>artha-śakti-mūla</s>), since the expressed meaning and the meaning inferred from its capacity are entirely different from each other, the cause-effect relationship between those two cognitions cannot be denied — thus the temporal sequence is clearly evident, as in the Prakrit <s>gāthās</s> cited in the first <s>uddyota</s> as illustrations for establishing suggested meaning. And in such cases, since the expressed and the suggested are entirely different, one cannot say that the very cognition of one is identical with the cognition of the other. In <s>dhvani</s> of the reverberation type rooted in the power of the word (<s>śabda-śakti-mūla</s>) — as in 'May the cows of you purifiers generate the utmost delight' and the like — since the cognition of the two meanings is verbal, the cognition of the simile-comparand (<s>upamāna-upameya</s>) relationship between the two meanings arises from the capacity of the meaning in the absence of an explicit word denoting simile — thus even there, the temporal sequence between the cognitions of the expressed and the suggested <s>alaṅkāra</s> is clearly discernible. In <s>dhvani</s> of the reverberation type rooted in the power of the word through word-illumination (<s>pada-prakāśa-śabda-śakti-mūla</s>) as well — since the joining of a qualifying word capable of relating to both meanings, without an explicit connective word, is established from the meaning itself even though non-verbal — here too, as before, the temporal sequence between the cognitions of the expressed and the <s>alaṅkāra</s> inferred from its capacity is well established. And even the cognition based on meaning in such a case is deemed to be rooted in the power of the word, because it is generated by the capacity of the word that is capable of relating to both meanings.

children.text: avivakṣita-vācyasya tu dhvaneḥ prasiddha-sva-viṣaya-vaimukhya-pratīti-pūrvakam evārthāntara-prakāśanam iti niyama-bhāvī kramaḥ / tatrāvivakṣita-vācyatvād eva vācyena saha vyaṅgyasya krama-pratīti-vicāro na kṛtaḥ / tasmād abhidhānābhidheya-pratītyor iva vācya-vyaṅgya-pratītyor nimitta-nimitti-bhāvān niyama-bhāvī kramaḥ / sa tūkta-yuktyā kvacil lakṣyate kvacin na lakṣyate /
children.translated_text: But in the case of <s>dhvani</s> where the expressed meaning is unintended (<s>avivakṣita-vācya</s>), the illumination of another meaning takes place only after the cognition of the aversion from the well-known domain of the expressed meaning — thus there is an invariable sequence. There, precisely because the expressed meaning is unintended, the examination of the sequential cognition of the suggested together with the expressed was not undertaken. Therefore, just as between denotation (<s>abhidhāna</s>) and the cognition of the denoted (<s>abhidheya</s>), so too between the cognitions of the expressed and the suggested, there is an invariable sequence due to the cause-effect relationship. That [sequence], however, as has been argued, is in some cases perceptible and in some cases imperceptible.

children.text: tad evaṃ vyañjaka-mukhena dhvani-prakāreṣu nirūpiteṣu kaścid brūyāt-kim idaṃ vyañjakatvaṃ nāma vyaṅgyārtha-prakāśanam, na hi vyañjakatvam / tad vyaṅgyatvaṃ cārthasya vyañjaka-siddhy-adhīnaṃ vyaṅgyatvam / vyaṅgyāpekṣayā ca vyañjakatva-siddhir ity anyonya-saṃśrayād avyavasthānam / nanu vācya-vyatiriktasya vyaṅgyasya siddhiḥ prāg eva pratipāditā tat-siddhy-adhīnā ca vyañjaka-siddhir iti kaḥ paryanuyogāvasaraḥ /
children.translated_text: Now, when the varieties of <s>dhvani</s> have been thus examined through the suggestor (<s>vyañjaka</s>) — someone might say: 'What is this so-called suggestive power (<s>vyañjakatva</s>)? Is it the illumination of the suggested meaning? Surely that is not suggestive power per se. And the suggested-ness (<s>vyaṅgyatva</s>) of a meaning depends on the establishment of the suggestor; while the establishment of the suggestor depends on the suggested — thus, from mutual dependence (<s>anyonya-āśraya</s>), there is indeterminacy.' [Reply:] But surely the existence of the suggested as something distinct from the expressed was already demonstrated earlier, and the establishment of the suggestor depends on that [prior demonstration] — so where is the occasion for objection?

children.text: satyam evaitat / prāg-ukta-yuktibhir vācya-vyatiriktasya vastunaḥ siddhiḥ kṛtā, sa tv artho vyaṅgyatayaiva kasmād vyapadiśyate yatra ca prādhānyenānavasthānaṃ tatra vācyatayaivāsau vyapadeṣṭuṃ yuktaḥ, tat-paratvād vākyasya / ataś ca tat-prakāśino vākyasya vācakatvam eva vyāpāraḥ / kiṃ tasya vyāpārāntara-kalpanayā ? tasmāt tātparya-viṣayo yo 'rthaḥ sa tāvan mukhyatayā vācyaḥ / yā tv antarā tathā-vidhe viṣaye vācyāntara-pratītiḥ sā tat-pratīter upāya-mātraṃ padārtha-pratītiriva vākyārtha-pratīteḥ /
children.translated_text: That is indeed true. Through the arguments stated earlier, the existence of a reality distinct from the expressed meaning has been established. However, why should that meaning be designated specifically as 'suggested' (<s>vyaṅgya</s>)? And where it does not exist primarily [i.e., where it is not the main purport], that [meaning] should properly be designated as 'expressed' (<s>vācya</s>), since the sentence is directed toward it. And accordingly, the function of the sentence that illuminates it is merely denotation (<s>vācakatva</s>). What is the point of postulating another function for it? Therefore, the meaning that is the purport [of the sentence] is primarily the expressed meaning. But the intervening cognition of another expressed meaning in such a case is merely a means toward the cognition of that [purported meaning] — just as the cognition of word-meanings [is a means] toward the cognition of sentence-meaning.

children.text:
atrocyate-yatra śabdaḥ svārtham abhidadhāno 'rthāntaram avagamayati tatra yat tasya svārthābhidhāyitvaṃ yac ca tadarthāntarāvagama-hetutvaṃ tayor aviśeṣo viśeṣo vā / na tāvad aviśeṣaḥ; yasmāt tau dvau vyāpārau bhinna-viṣayau bhinna-rūpau ca pratīyete eva / tathā hi vācakatva-lakṣaṇo vyāpāraḥ śabdasya svārtha-viṣayaḥ gamakatva-lakṣaṇas tv arthāntara-viṣayaḥ / na ca sva-para-vyavahāro vācya-vyaṅgyayor apahnotuṃ śakyaḥ, ekasya sambandhitvena pratīter aparasya sambandhi-sambandhitvena / vācyo hy arthaḥ sākṣāc-chabdasya sambandhī tad-itaras tv abhidheya-sāmarthyākṣiptaḥ sambandhi-sambandhī / yadi ca sva-sambandhitvaṃ sākṣāt tasya syāt tadārthāntaratva-vyavahāra eva na syāt / tasmād viṣaya-bhedas tāvat tayor vyāpārayoḥ suprasiddhaḥ / rūpa-bhedo 'pi prasiddha eva / na hi yaivābhidhāna-śaktiḥ saivāvagamana-śaktiḥ / avācakasyāpi gīta-śabdāde rasādi-lakṣaṇārthāvagama-darśanāt / aśabdasyāpi ceṣṭāder artha-viśeṣa-prakāśana-prasiddheḥ / tathā hi "vrīḍā-yogān natavadanayā" ity ādiśloke ceṣṭāviśeṣaḥ sukavinārtha-prakāśanahetuḥ pradarśita eva / tasmād bhinna-viṣayatvādbhinna-rūpatvāc ca svārthābhidhāyitvam arthāntarāvagama-hetutvaṃ ca śabdasya yat tayoḥ spaṣṭa eva bhedaḥ / viśeṣaś cen na tarhīdānīm avagamanasyābhidheya-sāmarthyākṣiptasyārthāntarasya vācyatva-vyapadeśyatā /
śabda-vyāpāra-gocaratvaṃ tu tasyāsmābhir iṣyata eva, tat tu vyaṅgyatvenaiva na vācyatvena /
prasiddhābhidhānāntara-sambandha-yogyatvena ca tasyārthāntarasya pratīteḥ śabdāntareṇa svārthābhidhāyinā yad-viṣayīkaraṇaṃ tatra prakāśanoktir eva yuktā /
na ca padārtha-vākyārtha-nyāyo vācya-vyaṅgyayoḥ / yataḥ padārtha-pratītir asatyaiveti kaiścid vidvadbhir āsthitam / yair apy asatyatvam asyā nābhyupeyate tair vākyārtha-padārthayor ghaṭa-tad-upādāna-kāraṇa-nyāyo 'bhyupagantavyaḥ / yathā hi ghaṭe niṣpanne tad-upādāna-kāraṇānāṃ na pṛthag-upalambhas tathaiva vākye tad-arthe vā pratīte pada-tad-arthānāṃ teṣāṃ tadā vibhaktatayopalambhe vākyārtha-buddhir eva dūrībhavet / na tv eṣa vācya-vyaṅgyayor nyāyaḥ, na hi vyaṅgye pratīyamāne vācya-buddhir dūrībhavati, vācyāvabhāsāvinābhāvena tasya prakāśanāt / tasmād ghaṭa-pradīpa-nyāyas tayoḥ, yathaiva hi pradīpa-dvāreṇa ghaṭa-pratītāv utpannāyāṃ na pradīpa-prakāśo nivartate tad-vyaṅgya-pratītau vācyāvabhāsaḥ / yat tu prathamoddyote "yathā padārtha-dvāreṇa" (1.10) ity ādy-uktaṃ tad-upāyatva-mātrāt sāmya-vivakṣayā /
children.translated_text: To this we reply: Where a word, while denoting its own meaning, causes the apprehension of another meaning — there, its property of denoting its own meaning and its property of causing the apprehension of that other meaning are either identical or distinct. They are not, to begin with, identical; for those two operations are perceived as having different domains and different forms. For the operation characterized as denotation (<s>vācakatva</s>) has the word's own meaning as its domain, while the operation characterized as causing apprehension (<s>gamakatva</s>) has the other meaning as its domain. And the distinction of 'own' and 'other' between the expressed (<s>vācya</s>) and the suggested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>) cannot be denied, since one is apprehended as directly related to the word, while the other is related to what is related [to the word]. For the expressed meaning is directly related to the word, while the other [meaning], evoked by the capacity of the expressed, is related to what is related [to the word]. And if it were directly related to the word itself, the very designation 'other meaning' would not apply. Therefore, the difference in domain between those two operations is well established. The difference in form, too, is well established. For the power of denotation is not the same as the power of causing apprehension, since even non-denotative [sounds] like musical tones are seen to produce the apprehension of meanings characterized as <s>rasa</s> and the like. And even non-verbal [signs] such as gestures are well-known to manifest specific meanings. As indeed, in the verse 'With downcast face due to modesty,' a particular gesture was shown by the good poet as a cause for manifesting meaning. Therefore, since the word's property of denoting its own meaning and its property of causing the apprehension of another meaning differ in both domain and form, the distinction between them is clear. And if there is a distinction, then the other meaning, apprehended through the capacity of the expressed, should not be designated as 'expressed' (<s>vācya</s>). We do indeed accept that it falls within the operation of the word, but as suggested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>), not as expressed. And since that other meaning is apprehended through its fitness for connection with a well-known different denotation, when it is made the object [of apprehension] by another word that denotes its own meaning, the characterization as 'manifestation' (<s>prakāśana</s>) is appropriate. Moreover, the analogy of word-meaning and sentence-meaning does not apply to the expressed and the suggested. For some scholars hold that the apprehension of word-meaning is itself unreal [when the sentence-meaning is grasped]. And even those who do not accept its unreality must accept the analogy of a pot and its material cause for sentence-meaning and word-meanings: just as when a pot has been produced, its material causes are not perceived separately — so too, when a sentence or its meaning has been apprehended, if the words and their meanings were then perceived separately, the cognition of the sentence-meaning itself would be displaced. But this is not the analogy for the expressed and the suggested; for when the suggested is being apprehended, the cognition of the expressed is not displaced, since the suggested is manifested precisely through the inseparability of the expressed's appearance. Therefore, the analogy for them is that of a pot and a lamp: just as when the apprehension of a pot has arisen through the medium of a lamp, the light of the lamp does not cease — so too, the appearance of the expressed [does not cease] when the suggested is apprehended. As for what was stated in the First <s>Uddyota</s> — 'just as through the medium of word-meaning' (1.10) and so forth — that was said with the intention of [showing] mere similarity in being a means.

children.text: nanv evaṃ yugapad-artha-dvaya-yogitvaṃ vākyasya prāptaṃ tad-bhāve ca tasya vākyataiva vighaṭate, tasyā aikārthya-lakṣaṇatvāt ; naiṣa doṣaḥ ; guṇa-pradhāna-bhāvena tayor vyavasthānāt / vyaṅgyasya hi kvacit prādhānyaṃ vācyasyopasarjana-bhāvaḥ kvacid vācyasya prādhānyam aparasya guṇa-bhāvaḥ / tatra vyaṅgya-prādhānye dhvanir ity uktam eva ; vācya-prādhānye tu prakārāntaraṃ nirdekṣyate / tasmāt sthitam etat-vyaṅgya-paratve 'pi kāvyasya na vyaṅgyasyābhidheyatvam api tu vyaṅgyatvam eva /
children.translated_text: Now, [the objection:] 'In this case, the sentence's connection with two meanings simultaneously would follow, and if that were so, its very sentence-hood would collapse, since sentence-hood is defined by unity of meaning (<s>aikārthya</s>).' This is not a defect, because those two [meanings] are established in the relation of principal and subsidiary. For the suggested is primary in some cases and the expressed is subsidiary, while in other cases the expressed is primary and the other [suggested] is subsidiary. When the suggested is primary, it has been called <s>dhvani</s>, as already stated; when the expressed is primary, another category will be specified. Therefore, it stands that even when the suggested is primary in poetry, the suggested does not become 'expressed' — it remains precisely 'suggested.'

children.text: kiṃ ca vyaṅgyasya prādhānyenāvivakṣāyāṃ vācyatvaṃ tāvad bhavadbhir nābhyupagantavyam atatparatvāc chabdasya / tad asti tāvad vyaṅgyaḥ śabdānāṃ kaścid viṣaya iti / yatrāpi tasya prādhānyaṃ tatrāpi kim iti tasya svarūpam apahnūyate / evaṃ tāvad vācakatvād anyad eva vyañjakatvam ; itaś ca vācakatvād vyañjakatvasyānyatvaṃ yad vācakatvaṃ śabdaikāśrayam itarat tu śabdāśrayam arthāśrayaṃ ca śabdārthayor dvayor api vyañjakatvasya pratipāditatvāt /
children.translated_text: Moreover, when the suggested is not intended to be primary, you [opponents] should not accept it as 'expressed,' since the word is not directed toward it. So there does exist some domain of words that is 'suggested.' And even where it is primary, why should its true nature be denied? Thus, to begin with, suggestive power (<s>vyañjakatva</s>) is indeed something other than denotation (<s>vācakatva</s>). And furthermore, the otherness of suggestive power from denotation [is seen in this:] denotation resides in words alone, whereas the other [suggestive power] resides in both words and meanings — since the suggestive power of both words and meanings has been demonstrated.

children.text: guṇa-vṛttis tūpacāreṇa lakṣaṇayā cobhayāśrayāpi bhavati / kintu tato 'pi vyañjakatvaṃ svarūpato viṣayataś ca bhidyate / rūpa-bhedas tāvad ayam-yad amukhyatayā vyāpāro guṇa-vṛttiḥ prasiddhā / vyañjakatvaṃ tu mukhyatayaiva śabdasya vyāpāraḥ / na hy arthād vyaṅgya-traya-pratītir yā tasyā amukhyatvaṃ manāg api lakṣyate /
children.translated_text: Secondary usage (<s>guṇa-vṛtti</s>), however — whether through figurative transfer (<s>upacāra</s>) or indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) — can also reside in both [words and meanings]. But suggestive power differs from it too, both in nature and in domain. The difference in nature is this: the operation [called] secondary usage is well-known as non-primary. But suggestive power is a primary operation of the word. For in the apprehension of the threefold suggested [<s>rasa</s>, <s>alaṅkāra</s>, <s>vastu</s>] from the meaning, not the slightest non-primariness is observed.

children.text: ayaṃ cānyaḥ svarūpa-bhedaḥ-yad guṇa-vṛttir amukhyatvena vyavasthitaṃ vācakatvam evocyate / vyañjakatvaṃ tu vācakatvād atyantaṃ vibhinnam eva / etac ca pratipāditam / ayaṃ cāparo rūpa-bhedo yadguṇa-vṛttau yadārtho 'rthāntaram upalakṣayati tadopalakṣaṇīyārthātmanā pariṇata evāsau sampadyate / yathā "gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ" ity ādau / vyañjakatva-mārge tu yadārtho 'rthāntaraṃ dyotayati tadā svarūpaṃ prakāśayann evāsāv anyasya prakāśakaḥ pratīyate pradīpavat / yathā-"līlā-kamala-patrāṇi gaṇayāmāsa pārvatī" ity ādau / yadi ca yatrātiraskṛtasva-pratītir artho 'rthāntaraṃ lakṣayati tatra lakṣaṇā-vyavahāraḥ kriyate, tad evaṃ sati lakṣaṇaiva mukhyaḥ śabda-vyāpāra iti prāptam / yasmāt prāyeṇa vākyānāṃ vācya-vyatirikta-tātparya-viṣayārthāvabhāsitvam /
children.translated_text: And here is another difference in nature: secondary usage is said to be denotation itself, established as non-primary. But suggestive power is utterly distinct from denotation — and this has been demonstrated. And here is yet another difference in nature: in secondary usage, when a meaning indicates another meaning, it transforms into the form of the indicated meaning. As in '<s>Gaṅgā</s>-on the village' [meaning 'on the bank of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>'] and the like. But in the path of suggestive power, when a meaning illuminates another meaning, it is perceived as illuminating that other while manifesting its own form — like a lamp. As in '<s>Pārvatī</s> counted the petals of the play-lotus' and the like. And if the usage of indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) were applied wherever a meaning, without suppressing its own apprehension, indicates another meaning, then it would follow that indication alone is the primary operation of words — since sentences predominantly manifest meanings other than the expressed as their purport.

children.text: nanu tvat-pakṣe 'pi yadārtho vyaṅgya-trayaṃ prakāśayati tadā śabdasya kīdṛśo vyāpāraḥ ? ucyate-prakaraṇādy-avacchinna-śabda-vaśenaivārthasya tathā-vidhaṃ vyañjakatvam iti śabdasya tatropayogaḥ katham apahnūyate ?
children.translated_text: Now, [the objection:] 'On your view too, when the meaning manifests the threefold suggested, what kind of operation does the word have?' We reply: Since the meaning's suggestive power of that kind arises precisely through the force of the word as delimited by context and the like, how can the word's contribution there be denied?

children.text: viṣaya-bhedo 'pi guṇa-vṛtti-vyañjakatvayoḥ spaṣṭa eva / yato vyañjakatvasya rasādayo 'laṅkāra-viśeṣā vyaṅgya-rūpāvacchinnaṃ vastu ceti trayaṃ viṣayaḥ / tatra rasādi-pratītir guṇa-vṛttir iti na kenacid ucyate na ca śakyate vaktum / vyaṅgyālaṅkāra-pratītir api tathaiva / vastu-cārutva-pratītaye sva-śabdānabhidheyatvena yat pratipipādayitum iṣyate tad vyaṅgyam / tac ca na sarvaṃ guṇa-vṛtterviṣayaḥ prasiddhy-anurodhābhyām api gauṇānāṃ śabdānāṃ prayoga-darśanāt / tathoktaṃ prāk / yadapi ca guṇa-vṛtter viṣayastad api ca vyañjakatvānupraveśena / tasmād guṇa-vṛtter api vyañjakatvasyātyanta-vilakṣaṇatvam / vācakatva-guṇa-vṛtti-vilakṣaṇasyāpi ca tasya tad-ubhayāśrayatvena vyavasthānam /
children.translated_text: The difference in domain between secondary usage and suggestive power too is perfectly clear. For the domain of suggestive power is threefold: <s>rasa</s> and the like, particular figures of speech (<s>alaṅkāra-viśeṣa</s>), and subject-matter delimited by suggestive form (<s>vastu</s>). Among these, the apprehension of <s>rasa</s> and the like is not called 'secondary usage' by anyone, nor can it be so called. The apprehension of suggested figures likewise. As for what is intended to be communicated as charming subject-matter that is not expressed by its own word — that is the suggested. And not all of that is the domain of secondary usage, since the use of figurative words is also seen in conformity with convention and propriety. So it was stated earlier. And even what is the domain of secondary usage is so through the entry of suggestive power. Therefore, suggestive power is utterly distinct from secondary usage. And although it is utterly distinct from both denotation and secondary usage, it is established as residing in both.

children.text: vyañjakatvaṃ hi kvacid vācakatvāśrayeṇa vyavatiṣṭhate, yathā vivakṣitānya-para-vācye dhvanau / kvacit tu guṇa-vṛtty-āśrayeṇa yathā avivakṣita-vācye dhvanau / tad-ubhayāśrayatva-pratipādanāyaiva ca dhvaneḥ prathamataraṃ dvau prabhedāv upanyastau / tad ubhayāśritatvāc ca tad-eka-rūpatvaṃ tasya na śakyate vaktum / yasmān na tad-vācakatvaika-rūpam eva, kvacil lakṣaṇāśrayeṇa vṛtteḥ / na ca lakṣaṇaika-rūpam evānyatra vācakatvāśrayeṇa vyavasthānāt / na cobhaya-dharmatvenaiva tad-ekaika-rūpaṃ na bhavati / yāvad vācakatva-lakṣaṇādi-rūpa-rahita-śabd-adharmatvenāpi / tathā hi gīta-dhvanīnām api vyañjakatvam asti rasādi-viṣayam / na ca teṣāṃ vācakatvaṃ lakṣaṇā vā kathañcil lakṣyate / śabdād anyatrāpi viṣaye vyañjakatvasya darśanād vācakatvādi-śabda-dharma-prakāratvam ayuktaṃ vaktum / yadi ca vācakatva-lakṣaṇādīnāṃ śabda-prakārāṇāṃ prasiddha-prakāra-vilakṣaṇatve 'pi vyañjakatvaṃ prakāratvena parikalpyate tac chabdasyaiva prakāratvena kasmān na parikalpyate ?
children.translated_text: For suggestive power sometimes subsists by resting on denotation, as in <s>dhvani</s> whose expressed meaning is intended but directed toward another [the suggested]. And sometimes it subsists by resting on secondary usage, as in <s>dhvani</s> whose expressed meaning is not intended. And it is precisely to demonstrate its resting on both that the two varieties of <s>dhvani</s> were presented at the very outset. And because it rests on both, it cannot be said to be identical in nature with either one. For it is not identical in nature with denotation alone, since sometimes it functions through indication. Nor is it identical with indication alone, since elsewhere it is established by resting on denotation. Nor is it the case that, merely by having the properties of both, it cannot have its own distinct nature — since it exists as a property of words that is devoid of the forms of denotation and indication and the like. For even musical tones have suggestive power with respect to <s>rasa</s> and the like, and yet neither denotation nor indication is in any way observed in them. And since suggestive power is seen even in domains other than words, it is improper to say it is merely a type of verbal property like denotation. And if suggestive power is posited as a type [of verbal function] even though it differs from the well-known types of verbal functions like denotation and indication — why should it not be posited as a type of the word itself?

children.text: tad evaṃ śābde vyavahāre trayaḥ prakārāḥ-vācakatvaṃ guṇa-vṛttir vyañjakatvaṃ ca / tatra vyañjakatve yadā vyaṅgya-prādhānyaṃ tadā dhvaniḥ, tasya cāvivakṣita-vācyo vivakṣitānya-para-vācyaś ceti dvau prabhedāv anukrāntau prathamataraṃ tau savistaraṃ nirṇītau /
children.translated_text: Thus, in verbal communication (<s>śābda-vyavahāra</s>), there are three types [of function]: denotation (<s>vācakatva</s>), secondary usage (<s>guṇa-vṛtti</s>), and suggestive power (<s>vyañjakatva</s>). Among these, when the suggested is primary within the domain of suggestive power, that is <s>dhvani</s>. And its two varieties — <s>dhvani</s> whose expressed meaning is unintended (<s>avivakṣita-vācya</s>) and <s>dhvani</s> whose expressed meaning is intended but directed toward another (<s>vivakṣitānya-para-vācya</s>) — were enumerated at the outset and have been discussed in detail.

children.text: anyo brūyāt-nanu vivakṣitānya-para-vācye dhvanau guṇa-vṛttitā nāstīti yad ucyate tad yuktam / yasmād vācya-vācaka-pratīti-pūrvikā yatrārthāntara-pratipattis tatra kathaṃ guṇa-vṛtti-vyavahāraḥ, na hi guṇa-vṛttau yadā nimittena kenacid viṣayāntare śabda āropyate atyanta-tiraskṛta-svārthaḥ / yathā-"agnir māṇavakaḥ" ity ādau, yadā vā svārtham aṃśenāparityajaṃs tat-sambandha-dvāreṇa viṣayāntaram ākrāmati, yathā "gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ" ity ādau / tadāvivakṣita-vācyatvam upapadyate / ata eva ca vivakṣitānya-para-vācye dhvanau vācya-vācakayor dvayor api svarūpa-pratītir arthāvagamanaṃ ca dṛśyata iti vyañjakatva-vyavahāro yukty-anurodhī / svarūpaṃ prakāśayann eva parāvabhāsako vyañjaka ity ucyate, tathāvidhe viṣaye vācakatvasyaiva vyañjakatvam iti guṇa-vṛtti-vyavahāro niyamenaiva na śakyate kartum / avivakṣita-vācyas tu dhvanir guṇa-vṛtteḥ kathaṃ bhidyate ? tasya prabheda-dvaye guṇa-vṛttiprabhedadvaya-rūpatā lakṣyata eva yataḥ /
children.translated_text: Another might say: 'Now, it is rightly stated that there is no secondary usage in <s>dhvani</s> whose expressed meaning is intended but directed toward another. For where the apprehension of another meaning is preceded by the apprehension of the expressed and the expressor, how can the designation of secondary usage apply? For secondary usage does not apply where a word, with its own meaning completely set aside, is superimposed upon another domain by some ground — as in "The boy is [a] fire" and the like; nor where a word, without entirely abandoning its own meaning, proceeds to another domain through the connection with that [own meaning] — as in "The village on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>" and the like. In that case, the status of unintended expressed meaning is established. And precisely for this reason, in <s>dhvani</s> whose expressed meaning is intended but directed toward another, the apprehension of the true form and the apprehension of meaning of both the expressed and the expressor are observed — hence the designation of suggestive power is consistent with reason. For [a word] is called a suggestor (<s>vyañjaka</s>) when it manifests another while revealing its own form — in such a domain, since it is denotation itself that functions as suggestive power, the designation of secondary usage simply cannot be applied. But as for <s>dhvani</s> whose expressed meaning is unintended — how does it differ from secondary usage? For in both its sub-varieties, the form of the two sub-varieties of secondary usage is indeed observed.'

children.text: ayam api na doṣaḥ / yasmād avivakṣita-vācyo dhvanir guṇa-vṛtti-mārgāśrayo 'pi bhavati na tu guṇa-vṛtti-rūpa eva / guṇa-vṛttir hi vyañjakatva-śūnyāpi dṛśyate / vyañjakatvaṃ ca yathokta-cārutva-hetuṃ vyaṅgyaṃ vinā na vyavatiṣṭhate / guṇa-vṛttis tu vācya-dharmāśrayeṇaiva vyaṅgya-mātrāśrayeṇa cābhedopacāra-rūpā sambhavati, yathā-tīkṣṇatvād agnir māṇavakaḥ, āhlādakatvāc candra evāsyā mukham ity ādau / yathā ca "priye jane nāsti punar uktam" ity ādau / yāpi lakṣaṇa-rūpa-guṇa-vṛttiḥ sāpy upalakṣaṇīyārtha-saṃbandha-mātrāśrayeṇa cāru-rūpa-vyaṅgya-pratītiṃ vināpi sambhavaty eva, yathā-"mañcāḥ krośanti" ity ādau viṣaye /
children.translated_text: This too is not a defect. For <s>dhvani</s> whose expressed meaning is unintended, while taking the path of secondary usage (<s>guṇa-vṛtti</s>), is not identical in nature with secondary usage. For secondary usage is seen to exist even devoid of suggestive power. And suggestive power does not subsist without the suggested, which is the cause of the characteristic charm. Secondary usage, however, based merely on the property of the expressed and on mere indication, can take the form of non-differentiating transference — as in 'The boy is a fire, due to his sharpness,' or 'Her face is the moon itself, due to its delightfulness' and the like; and as in 'There is no repetition when [speaking of] a beloved person' and the like. And even the indication-type secondary usage can perfectly well exist, based merely on the connection with the indicated meaning, without the apprehension of the charming suggested — as in 'The platforms are crying out' and the like.

children.text: yatra tu sā cāru-rūpa-vyaṅgya-pratīti-hetus tatrāpi vyañjakatvānupraveśenaiva vācakatvavat / asambhavinā cārthena yatra vyavahāraḥ, yathā-"suvarṇa-puṣpāṃ pṛthivīm" ity ādau tatra cāru-rūpa-vyaṅgya-pratītir eva prayojiketi tathā-vidhe 'pi viṣaye guṇa-vṛttau satyām api dhvani-vyavahāra eva yukty-anurodhī / tasmād avivakṣita-vācye dhvanau dvayor api prabhedayor vyañjakatva-viśeṣāviśiṣṭā guṇa-vṛttir na tu tad-eka-rūpā sahṛdaya-hṛdayāhlādinī pratīyamānā pratīti-hetutvād viṣayāntare tad-rūpa-śūnyāyā darśanāt / etac ca sarvaṃ prāk sūcitam api sphuṭatara-pratītaye punar uktam /
children.translated_text: But where that [composition] is the cause of the apprehension of a beautiful suggested meaning — there too, the operation is only through the entry of suggestive power (<s>vyañjakatva</s>), just as with denotative power (<s>vācakatva</s>). Where there is usage involving a meaning that is impossible [as literal denotation], as in 'the golden-flowered earth' and the like — there the apprehension of the beautiful suggested meaning alone is the motivating [factor]. Therefore, even in such a domain, when the subordinate figurative function (<s>guṇa-vṛtti</s>) is present, the designation of <s>dhvani</s> alone is consistent with reason. Therefore, in <s>dhvani</s> where the expressed meaning is unintended (<s>avivakṣita-vācya</s>), the subordinate figurative function, which is not different [in kind] from the specific suggestive power in both varieties [of this dhvani], is not identical with it [either] — for it is perceived as delighting the hearts of the sensitive (<s>sahṛdaya</s>), because it is the cause of [aesthetic] apprehension, whereas in other domains it is seen to be devoid of that character. And all this, though previously indicated, is restated for greater clarity of understanding.

children.text: api ca vyañjakatva-lakṣaṇo yaḥ śabdārthayor dharmaḥ sa prasiddha-sambandhānurodhīti na kasyacid vimati-viṣayatām arhati / śabdārthayor hi prasiddho yaḥ sambandho vācya-vācaka-bhāvākhyas tam anurundhāna eva vyañjakatva-lakṣaṇo vyāpāraḥ sāmagry-antara-sambandhād aupādhikaḥ pravartate / ata eva vācakatvāt tasya viśeṣaḥ / vācakatvaṃ hi śabda-viśeṣasya niyata ātmā vyutpatti-kālād ārabhya tad-avinābhāvena tasya prasiddhatvāt / sa tv aniyataḥ, aupādhikatvāt / prakaraṇādy-avacchedena tasya pratīter itarathā tv apratīteḥ /
children.translated_text: Moreover, the property of words and meanings that is characterized as suggestive power (<s>vyañjakatva</s>) follows established convention and therefore ought not be the subject of anyone's disagreement. For the verbal operation characterized as suggestive power, while conforming to the established relation between word and meaning known as the expresser-expressed relationship (<s>vācya-vācaka-bhāva</s>), operates adventitiously (<s>aupādhika</s>) through a connection with additional conditions (<s>sāmagrī</s>). And precisely because of this, it differs from denotative power (<s>vācakatva</s>). For the denotative power of a particular word is its fixed nature, since from the time of learning [the word-meaning relation], it is known as inseparable from it. But that [suggestive power] is unfixed, being adventitious — for it is apprehended only when delimited by context and the like, and not otherwise.

children.text:
nanu yady aniyatas tat kiṃ tasya svarūpa-parīkṣayā ? naiṣa doṣaḥ ; yataḥ śabdātmani tasyāniyatatvam, na tu sve viṣaye vyaṅgya-lakṣaṇe / liṅgatva-nyāyaś cāsya vyañjaka-bhāvasya lakṣyate, yathā liṅgatvam āśrayeṣv aniyatāvabhāsam, icchādhīnatvāt ; sva-viṣayāvyabhicāri ca /
tathaivedaṃ yathā darśitaṃ vyañjakatvam / śabdātmany aniyatatvād eva ca tasya vācakatva-prakāratā na śakyā kalpayitum / yadi hi vācakatva-prakāratā tasya bhavet tac-chabdātmani niyatatāpi syād vācakatvavat / sa ca tathā-vidha aupādhiko dharmaḥ śabdānām autpattika-śabdārtha-sambandha-vādinā vākya-tattva-vidā pauruṣāpauruṣeyayor vākyayor viśeṣam abhidadhatā niyamenābhyupagantavyaḥ, tad anabhyupagame hi tasya śabdārtha-sambandha-nityatve saty apy apauruṣeya-pauruṣeyayor vākyayor artha-pratipādane nirviśeṣatvaṃ syāt /
tad-abhyupagame tu pauruṣeyāṇāṃ vākyānāṃ puruṣecchānuvidhāna-samāropitaupādhika-vyāpārāntarāṇāṃ saty api svābhidheya-sambandhāparityāge mithyārthatāpi bhavet /
children.translated_text: Objection: If it is unfixed, then what is the purpose of examining its nature? Reply: This is not a fault, for its unfixedness is with respect to the word as substrate, not with respect to its own domain — the suggested meaning (<s>vyaṅgya</s>). And the principle of indicativeness (<s>liṅgatva</s>) is observed [to be analogous] to this suggestive function: just as indicativeness appears unfixed in its substrates, being dependent on [the cognizer's] intention, yet is unerring with respect to its own object. Just so is this suggestive power as described. And precisely because of its unfixedness in the word as substrate, it cannot be conceived as a mode of denotative power. For if it were a mode of denotative power, then it would be fixed in the word as substrate, just as denotative power is. And this adventitious property of words must be necessarily accepted by one who knows the true nature of sentences, who holds that the word-meaning relation is innate (<s>autpattika</s>), and who posits a distinction between human (<s>pauruṣeya</s>) and non-human (<s>apauruṣeya</s>) sentences. For without accepting it, even though the word-meaning relation is eternal, there would be no difference between human and non-human sentences in conveying meaning. But with its acceptance, even though human sentences retain their connection with their own denotative meanings, false meaning (<s>mithyārthatā</s>) would also be possible for them — through adventitious additional operations imposed by conformity to human intention.

children.text: dṛśyate hi bhāvānām aparityakta-sva-svabhāvānām api sāmagry-antara-sampāta-sampāditaupādhika-vyāpārāntarāṇāṃ viruddha-kriyatvam / tathā hi-hima-mayūkha-prabhṛtīnāṃ nirvāpita-sakala-jīva-lokaṃ śītalatvam udvahatām eva priyā-viraha-dahana-dahyamāna-mānasair janair ālokyamānānāṃ satāṃ santāpa-kāritvaṃ prasiddham eva / tasmāt pauruṣeyāṇāṃ vākyānāṃ saty api naisargike 'rtha-sambandhe mithyārthatvaṃ samarthayitum icchatā vācakatva-vyatiriktaṃ kiṃcid rūpam aupādhikaṃ vyaktam evābhidhānīyam / tac ca vyañjakatvādṛte nānyat / vyaṅgya-prakāśanaṃ hi vyañjakatvam / pauruṣeyāṇi ca vākyāni prādhānyena puruṣābhiprāyam eva prakāśayanti / sa ca vyaṅgya eva na tv abhidheyaḥ, tena sahābhidhānasya vācya-vācakabhāva-lakṣaṇa-sambandhābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: For it is observed that entities, even without abandoning their own nature, perform contrary functions when an adventitious additional operation is produced through the conjunction of other conditions. For example, the moon's rays and the like — even while bearing their coolness that refreshes all living beings — are well known to cause torment when beheld by persons whose minds are being burned by the fire of separation from the beloved. Therefore, one who wishes to establish that human sentences can convey false meaning despite having an innate connection with [true] meaning must clearly acknowledge some adventitious form distinct from denotative power. And that is nothing other than suggestive power (<s>vyañjakatva</s>). For suggestive power is the illumination of the suggested meaning. And human sentences primarily illuminate the speaker's intention. That [intention] is indeed the suggested meaning, not the denoted meaning, since there is no connection characterized as the expresser-expressed relationship between the word and the [intention] together with [the denoted meaning].

children.text: nanv anena nyāyena sarveṣām eva laukikānāṃ vākyānāṃ dhvani-vyavahāraḥ prasaktaḥ / sarveṣām apy anena nyāyena vyañjakatvāt / satyam etat; kiṃ tu vaktr-abhiprāya-prakāśanena yad vyañjakatvaṃ tat sarveṣām eva laukikānāṃ vākyānām aviśiṣṭam / tat tu vācakatvān na bhidyate vyaṅgyam hi tatra nāntarīyakatayā vyavasthitam / na tu vivakṣitatvena / yasya tu vivakṣitatvena vyaṅgyasya sthitiḥ tad vyañjakatvaṃ dhvani-vyavahārasya prayojakam / yat tv abhiprāya-viśeṣa-rūpaṃ vyaṅgyaṃ śabdārthābhyāṃ prakāśate tad bhavati vivakṣitaṃ tātparyeṇa prakāśyamānaṃ sat / kintu tad eva kevalam aparimita-viṣayasya dhvani-vyavahārasya na prayojakam avyāpakatvāt / tathā darśita-bheda-traya-rūpaṃ tātparyeṇa dyotyamānam abhiprāya-rūpam anabhiprāya-rūpaṃ ca sarvam eva dhvani-vyavahārasya prayojakam iti yathokta-vyañjaktva-viśeṣe dhvani-lakṣaṇe nātivyāptir na cāvyāptiḥ / tasmād vākya-tattva-vidāṃ matena tāvad vyañjakatva-lakṣaṇaḥ śābdo vyāpāro na virodhī pratyutānuguṇa eva lakṣyate /
children.translated_text: Objection: By this reasoning, the designation of <s>dhvani</s> would apply to all ordinary sentences whatsoever, since all of them, by this reasoning, have suggestive power. Reply: This is true; however, the suggestive power that consists in illuminating the speaker's intention is common to all ordinary sentences without distinction. But that does not differ from denotative power, for the suggested [intention] there is not established as something independent — it is merely a necessary concomitant, not something specifically intended (<s>vivakṣita</s>). But where the suggested meaning has the status of being specifically intended — that suggestive power is the cause of the designation of <s>dhvani</s>. Now, the suggested [meaning] that takes the form of a specific intention and is illuminated by word and meaning — that becomes intended when it is illuminated with purposeful emphasis. But that alone is not sufficient to motivate the designation of <s>dhvani</s>, which has unlimited scope, since it is not coextensive [with all dhvani]. Rather, all that is illuminated with purposeful emphasis — whether in the form of intention or not, in the threefold division previously shown — all of this motivates the designation of <s>dhvani</s>. Thus, in the definition of <s>dhvani</s> as having the specific suggestive power described, there is neither over-extension nor under-extension. Therefore, according to the view of those who know the true nature of sentences, the verbal operation characterized as suggestive power is seen to be not at all opposed [to their doctrine], but rather consonant with it.

children.text: pariniścita-nirapa-bhraṃśa-śabda-brahmaṇāṃ vipaścitāṃ matam āśrityaiva pravṛtto 'yaṃ dhvani-vyavahāra iti taiḥ saha kiṃ virodhāvirodhau cintyete / kṛtrima-śabdārtha-sambandha-vādināṃ tu yukti-vidām anubhava-siddha evāyaṃ vyañjaka-bhāvaḥ śabdānām arthāntarāṇām ivāvirodhaś ceti na pratikṣepya-padavīm avatarati /
children.translated_text: This practice of <s>dhvani</s> has proceeded by relying on the view of the wise who have firmly established the infallible nature of <s>śabda-brahman</s> (the Word-Absolute). So what [need is there to] consider whether there is conflict or compatibility with them? For those of rational bent (<s>yukti-vid</s>) who hold that the word-meaning relation is conventional (<s>kṛtrima</s>), this suggestive function of words is simply established by experience, and [its] compatibility [with their view] is like [the compatibility] of other meanings — thus it does not enter the path of rejection.

children.text:
vācakatve hi tārkikāṇāṃ vipratipattayaḥ pravartantām, kim idaṃ svābhāvikaṃ śabdānām āho svit sāmayikam ity ādyāḥ / vyañjakatve tu tat-pṛṣṭha-bhāvini bhāvāntara-sādhāraṇe loka-prasiddha evānugamyamāne ko vimatīnām avasaraḥ / alaukike hy arthe tārkikāṇāṃ vimatayo nikhilāḥ pravartante na tu laukike / na hi nīla-madhurādiṣv aśeṣa-lokendriya-gocare bādhā-rahite tattve parasparaṃ vipratipannā dṛśyante / na hi bādhā-rahitaṃ nīlaṃ nīlam iti bruvann apareṇa pratiṣidhyate naitan nīlaṃ pītam etad iti / tathaiva vyañjakatvaṃ vācakānāṃ śabdānām avācakānāṃ ca gīta-dhvanīnām aśabda-rūpāṇāṃ ca ceṣṭādīnāṃ yat sarveṣām anubhava-siddham eva tat kenāpahnūyate / aśabdam arthaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ hi sūcayanto vyāhārās tathā vyāpārā nibaddhāś cānibaddhāś ca vidagdha-pariṣatsu vividhā vibhāvyante /
tān upahāsyatām ātmanaḥ pariharan ko 'tisandadhīta sacetāḥ /
children.translated_text: Regarding denotative power, let the logicians' disagreements proceed — whether it is natural to words or conventional, and so forth. But regarding suggestive power, which follows upon denotative power and is common to other entities as well, which is simply observed in common experience — what occasion is there for disagreement? For all the disagreements of logicians arise concerning objects beyond ordinary experience, not concerning ordinary ones. For with regard to blue, sweet, and the like — objects within the range of every person's senses, where there is no sublation — [people] are not seen to be mutually contradictory. For no one who says 'This undeniable blue is blue' is contradicted by another [saying] 'This is not blue, it is yellow.' Just so, the suggestive power of denotative words, and of non-denotative sounds such as musical tones, and of non-verbal [expressions] such as gestures and the like — that which is established by the experience of all — who can deny it? For various utterances and actions, both literary and non-literary, that indicate a charming unspoken meaning, are observed in assemblies of the refined. What sensitive person would try to deceive [others about this], inviting his own ridicule?

children.text: atha brūyāt, asty atisandhānāvasaraḥ vyañjakatvaṃ śabdānāṃ gamakatvaṃ tac ca liṅgatvam ataś ca vyaṅgya-pratītir liṅgi-pratītir eveti liṅgi-liṅga-bhāva eva teṣāṃ vyaṅgya-vyañjaka-bhāvo nāparaḥ kaścit / ataś caitad avaśyam eva boddhavyaṃ yasmād vaktr-abhiprāyāpekṣayā vyañjakatvam idānīm eva tvayā pratipāditaṃ vaktr-abhiprāyaś cānumeya-rūpa eva /
children.translated_text: If one were to say: 'There is indeed occasion for deception — the suggestive power of words is [simply their] indicative power (<s>gamakatva</s>), and that is [nothing but] <s>liṅgatva</s> (the power of a logical mark). Therefore the apprehension of the suggested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>) is merely the apprehension of the indicated (<s>liṅgin</s>). Thus the relation of suggested-and-suggestor is nothing but the relation of indicated-and-indicator, and nothing more. And this must necessarily be understood, since you yourself have just established suggestive power with reference to the speaker's intention, and the speaker's intention is of the nature of an inferential object.'

children.text: atrocyate-nanv evam api yadi nāma syāt tat kiṃ naś chinnam / vācakatva-guṇa-vṛtti-vyatirikto vyañjakatva-lakṣaṇaḥ śabda-vyāpāro 'stīty asmābhir abhyupagatam / tasya caivam api na kācit kṣatiḥ / tad dhi vyañjakatvaṃ liṅgatvam astu anyad vā / sarvathā prasiddha-śābda-prakāra-vilakṣaṇatvaṃ śabda-vyāpāra-viṣayatvaṃ ca tasyāstīti nāsty evāvayor vivādaḥ / na punar ayaṃ paramārtho yad-vyañjakatvaṃ liṅgatvam eva sarvatra vyaṅgya-pratītiś ca liṅgi-pratītir eveti /
children.translated_text: To this we say: Even if it were so, what of ours is thereby cut off? We have accepted that there exists a verbal operation characterized as suggestive power, distinct from denotative power and the subordinate figurative function. And even so, no harm comes to it. For let that suggestive power be <s>liṅgatva</s> (indicativeness) or something else — in all cases, its distinctness from the well-known modes of verbal [operation] and its being the object of verbal operation both exist. Thus there is no dispute between us at all. However, it is not actually the case that suggestive power is always [identical with] indicativeness, nor that the apprehension of the suggested is always inferential apprehension of the indicated.

children.text:
yad api sva-pakṣa-siddhaye 'smad-uktam anūditaṃ tvayā vaktr-abhiprāyasya vyaṅgyatvenābhyupagamāt tat-prakāśane śabdānāṃ liṅgatvam eveti tad etad yathāsmābhir abhihitaṃ tad vibhajyaṃ pratipādyate śrūyatām-dvividho viṣayaḥ śabdānāṃ-
anumeyaḥ pratipādyaś ca / tatrānumeyo vivakṣā-lakṣaṇaḥ / vivakṣā ca śabda-svarūpa-prakāśanecchā śabdenārtha-prakāśanecchā ceti dvi-prakārā / tatrādyā na śābda-vyavahārāṅgam / sā hi prāṇitva-mātra-pratipatti-phalā / dvitīyā tu śabda-viśeṣāvadhāraṇā-vasita-vyavahitāpi śabda-karaṇa-vyavahāra-nibandhanam / te tu dve apy anumeyo viṣayaḥ śabdānām / pratipādyas tu prayoktur artha-pratipādana-samīhā-viṣayīkṛto 'rthaḥ /
children.translated_text: As for what you have repeated from our own statement to establish your position — namely that since we accept the speaker's intention as the suggested, the words' function in revealing it is merely indicativeness — to that, we say: Let what we have stated be analyzed and presented — listen. Words have two kinds of object: the inferable and the communicable. Of these, the inferable is the intention (<s>vivakṣā</s>). And intention is of two kinds: the wish to manifest the word's own form, and the wish to manifest meaning through a word. Of these, the first is not a component of verbal practice; for its result is merely the cognition of a living being's [presence]. The second, though mediated by the ascertainment of a particular word, is the basis of the practice of using words as instruments. Both of these are the inferable object of words. The communicable, however, is the meaning that has been made the object of the user's effort to convey meaning.

children.text: sa ca dvividhaḥ-vācyo vyaṅgyaś ca / prayoktā hi kadācit sva-śabdenārthaṃ prakāśayituṃ samīhate kadācit sva-śabdānabhidheyatvena prayojanāpekṣayā kayācit / sa tu dvividho 'pi pratipādyo viṣayaḥ śabdānāṃ na liṅgitayā svarūpeṇa prakāśate, api tu kṛtrimeṇākṛtrimeṇa vā sambandhāntareṇa / vivakṣā-viṣayatvaṃ hi tasyārthasya śabdair liṅgitayā pratīyate na tu svarūpam / yadi hi liṅgitayā tatra śabdānāṃ vyāpāraḥ syāt tac chabdārthe samyaṅ mithyātvādi vivādā eva na pravarteran dhūmādi-liṅgānumitānumeyāntaravat / vyaṅgyaś cārtho vācya-sāmarthyākṣiptatayā vācyavac chabdasya sambandhī bhavaty eva / sākṣād-asākṣād-bhāvo hi sambandhasyāprayojakaḥ / vācya-vācaka-bhāvāśrayatvaṃ ca vyañjakatvasya prāg eva darśitam / tasmād vaktrabhiprāya-rūpa eva vyaṅgye liṅgatayā śabdānāṃ vyāpāraḥ / tad-viṣayīkṛte tu pratipādyatayā / pratīyamāne tasminn abhiprāya-rūpe 'nabhiprāya-rūpe ca vācakatve naiva vyāpāraḥ sambandhāntareṇa vā / na tāvad vācakatvena yathoktaṃ prāk / sambandhāntareṇa vyañjakatvam eva / na ca vyañjakatvaṃ liṅgatva-rūpam eva ālokādiṣv anyathā dṛṣṭatvāt / tasmāt pratipādyo viṣayaḥ śabdānāṃ na liṅgitvena sambandhī vācyavat / yo hi liṅgitvena teṣāṃ sambandhī yathā darśito viṣayaḥ sa na vācyatvena pratīyate, api tūpādhitvena / pratipādyasya ca viṣayasya liṅgitve tad-viṣayāṇāṃ vipratipattīnāṃ laukikair eva kriyamāṇānām abhāvaḥ prasajyeteti / etac coktam eva /
children.translated_text: And that [communicable meaning] is of two kinds: the expressed (<s>vācya</s>) and the suggested (<s>vyaṅgya</s>). For the user sometimes strives to illuminate meaning through his own word [directly], and sometimes through some purpose-dependent [means] by which the meaning is not directly denoted by his word. And this communicable object of words, even though twofold, does not manifest as an indicated thing (<s>liṅgin</s>) in its own form, but rather through some other connection — whether conventional or natural. For it is the object's status as the object of intention that is apprehended through words as an indicated thing — not its own form. For if the words' function there were that of an indicator, then disputes about the truth or falsity etc. of verbal meaning would never arise — just as they do not arise regarding [objects] inferred from smoke and other indicators. And the suggested meaning, being drawn forth by the capacity of the expressed, has a connection to the word just as the expressed meaning does. For directness or indirectness of the connection is irrelevant. And the dependence of suggestive power upon the expresser-expressed relationship has been shown previously. Therefore, it is only with respect to the suggested [meaning] in the form of the speaker's intention that words function as indicators. But with respect to the communicable [meaning] — the object [of communication] — there is no function through denotation, nor through any other connection [i.e., indication] alone, but rather through suggestive power. For suggestive power is not always of the form of indicativeness, since it is seen to operate differently in cases such as light and the like. Therefore, the communicable object of words is not connected [to them] as an indicated thing, unlike [the inferable]. For the domain that is connected to them as an indicated thing — as shown — is not apprehended as expressed, but rather as a condition (<s>upādhi</s>). And if the communicable object were connected through indicativeness, then the absence of disputes about it conducted by ordinary people — [disputes that do in fact exist] — would have to follow. And this has already been stated.

children.text: yathā ca vācya-viṣaye pramāṇāntarānugamena samyaktva-pratītau kvacit kriyamāṇāyāṃ tasya pramāṇāntara-viṣayatve saty api na śabda-vyāpāra-viṣayatā-hānis tad-vyaṅgyasyāpi / kāvya-viṣaye ca vyaṅgya-pratītīnāṃ satyā satya-nirūpaṇasyāprayojakatvam eveti tatra pramāṇāntara-vyāpāra-parīkṣopahāsāyaiva sampadyate / tasmāl liṅgi-pratītir eva sarvatra vyaṅgya-pratītir iti na śakyate vaktum /
children.translated_text: And just as in the domain of the expressed, when the correctness [of a cognition] is ascertained through corroboration by another means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇāntara</s>), even though [the meaning] is a valid object of that other means, there is no loss of its being an object of verbal operation—the same applies to what is suggested by it [i.e., words]. And in the domain of poetry, since the ascertainment of the truth or falsity of suggested cognitions serves no purpose, that [objection is refuted].

children.text: yat tv anumeya-rūpa-vyaṅgya-viṣayaṃ śabdānāṃ vyañjakatvaṃ tad-dhvani-vyavahārasyāprayojakam / api tu vyañjakatva-lakṣaṇaḥ śabdānāṃ vyāpāra autpattika-śabdārtha-sambandha-vādināpy abhyupagantavya iti pradarśanārtham upanyastam / tad dhi vyañjakatvaṃ kadācil liṅgatvena kadācid rūpāntareṇa śabdānāṃ vācakānām avācakānāṃ ca sarva-vādibhir apratikṣepyam ity ayam asmābhir yatna ārabdhaḥ / tad evaṃ guṇa-vṛtti-vācakatvādibhyaḥ śabda-prakārebhyo niyamenaiva tāvad vilakṣaṇaṃ vyañjakatvam / tad-antaḥ-pātitve 'pi tasya haṭhād abhidhīyamāne tad-viśeṣasya dhvaner yat-prakāśanaṃ vipratipatti-nirāsāya sahṛdaya-vyutpattaye vā tat-kriyamāṇam anatisandheyam eva / na hi sāmānya-mātra-lakṣaṇenopayogi-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇānāṃ pratikṣepaḥ śakyaḥ kartum / evaṃ hi sati sattā-mātra-lakṣaṇe kṛte sakala-sad-vastu-lakṣaṇānāṃ paunaruktya-prasaṅgaḥ / tad evam-
children.translated_text: However, the suggestive power (<s>vyañjakatva</s>) of words with respect to what is suggested in the form of the inferable (<s>anumeya-rūpa</s>) does not occasion the designation '<s>dhvani</s>.' Rather, it was adduced to demonstrate that the function of suggestion (<s>vyañjakatva</s>), which is the characteristic [power] of words, must be accepted even by those who hold the view that the relation between word and meaning is innate (<s>autpattika</s>). For that suggestive power is [merely inferential and thus does not constitute genuine dhvani].

children.text: vimati-viṣayo ya āsīn manīṣiṇāṃ satatam avidita-sa-tattvaḥ /
children.translated_text: That variety of poetry which was always the subject of disagreement among the wise, whose true nature was unknown—

children.text: dhvani-saṃjñitaḥ prakāraḥ kāvyasya vyañjitaḥ so 'yam || DhvA_3.33 ||
children.translated_text: That, designated as <s>dhvani</s>, has been elucidated here.
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 3.34:

children.text: prakāro 'nyo guṇī-bhūta-vyaṅgyaḥ kāvyasya dṛśyate /
children.translated_text: Another variety of poetry is observed, called <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s> (suggested-yet-subordinate),

children.text: yatra vyaṅgyānvaye vācya-cārutvaṃ syāt prakarṣavat // DhvK_3.34 //
children.translated_text: Where, even with the presence of the suggested, the charm of the expressed meaning is preeminent. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 3.34 //

children.text: vyaṅgyo 'rtho lalanā-lāvaṇya-prakhyo yaḥ pratipāditas tasya prādhānye dhvanir ity uktam / tasya tu guṇī-bhāvena vācya-cārutva-prakarṣe guṇī-bhūta-vyaṅgyo nāma kāvya-prabhedaḥ prakalpyate / tatra vastu-mātrasya vyaṅgyasya tiraskṛta-vācyebhyaḥ pratīyamānasya kadācid vācya-rūpa-vākyārthāpekṣayā guṇī-bhāve sati guṇī-bhūta-vyaṅgyatā / yathā-
children.translated_text: The suggested meaning has been demonstrated to be like the loveliness of a beautiful woman. When it has primacy, it was called <s>dhvani</s>. But when it becomes subordinate and the charm of the expressed meaning is preeminent, a variety of poetry called <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s> (suggested-yet-subordinate) is posited. In that [variety], the suggested, whether mere content (<s>vastu-mātra</s>) or [a figure], [is subordinate to the expressed]—

children.text: lāvaṇya-sindhur aparaiva hi keyam atra
children.translated_text: 'What other ocean of loveliness is this here,

children.text: yatrotpalāni śaśinā saha samplavante /
children.translated_text: Where lotuses float together with the moon,

children.text: unmajjati dvirada-kumbha-taṭī ca yatra
children.translated_text: Where the surface of an elephant's frontal globe rises up,

children.text: yatrāpare kadalikāṇḍa-mṛṇāla-daṇḍāḥ //
children.translated_text: And where there are other stems like plantain stalks and lotus fibers!'

children.text:
atiraskṛtavācyebhyo 'pi śabdebhyaḥ pratīyamānasya vyaṅgyasya kadācid vācya-prādhānyena kāvyacārutvāpekṣayā guṇībhāve sati guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyatā, yathodāhṛtam-"anurāgavatī sandhyā" ity evam ādi / tasyaiva svayam uktyā prakāśīkṛtatvena guṇībhāvaḥ, yathodāhṛtam-
"saṅketa-kāla-manasam" ity ādi / rasādi-rūpa-vyaṅgyasya guṇībhāvo rasavad-alaṅkāre darśitaḥ ; tatra ca teṣām ādhikārika-vākyāpekṣayā guṇībhāvo vivahana-pravṛtta-bhṛtyānuyāyi-rājavat / vyaṅgyālaṅkārasya guṇībhāve dīpakādi-viṣayaḥ || DhvA_3.34 ||
children.translated_text: Even from words whose expressed meaning is not obscured (<s>atiraskṛta-vācya</s>), the suggested element sometimes attains subordinate status (<s>guṇībhāva</s>) through the primacy of the expressed meaning with respect to the charm of poetry—that is <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s>. As has been cited: 'The twilight is full of passion (<s>anurāga</s>)'—and so forth. Its subordination [may be] through being rendered explicit by one's own utterance; as has been cited—

children.text: tathā-
children.translated_text: Likewise:
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 3.35:

children.text: prasanna-gambhīra-padāḥ kāvya-bandhāḥ sukhāvahāḥ /
children.translated_text: Poetic compositions that are lucid, profound in expression, and delightful—

children.text: ye ca teṣu prakāro 'yam eva yojyāḥ sumedhasā // DhvK_3.35 //
children.translated_text: In all of these, a person of keen intellect should apply this very variety [of guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya]. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 3.35 //

children.text: ye caite 'parimita-svarūpā api prakāśamānās tathāvidhārtha-ramaṇīyāḥ santo vivekināṃ sukhāvahāḥ kāvya-bandhās teṣu sarveṣv evāyaṃ prakāro guṇī-bhūta-vyaṅgyo nāma yojanīyaḥ / yathā-
children.translated_text: Those poetic compositions that, even while manifesting limitless forms and being charming with such meanings, are delightful to the discerning—in all of them, this variety called <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s> should be applied. For example:

children.text: lacchī duhidā jāmāuo harī taṃsa ghariṇiā gaṅgā /
children.translated_text: '<s>Lakṣmī</s> is the daughter, <s>Hari</s> the son-in-law, and <s>Gaṅgā</s> the wife,

children.text: amia-miaṅkā a suā aho kuḍumbaṃ mahoahiṇo //
children.translated_text: <s>Amṛta</s> (Nectar) and <s>Mṛgāṅka</s> (the Moon) are the sons—ah, what a family the great ocean has!'

children.text:
lakṣmī duhitā jāmātā hariḥ tathā gṛhiṇī gaṅgā /
amṛta-mṛgāṅkau ca sutau aho kuṭumbaṃ mahodadheḥ //
children.translated_text: '<s>Lakṣmī</s> is the daughter, <s>Hari</s> the son-in-law, and <s>Gaṅgā</s> the wife, <s>Amṛta</s> and <s>Mṛgāṅka</s> are the sons—ah, what a family the great ocean has!'
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 3.36:

children.text: vācyālaṅkāra-vargo 'yaṃ vyaṅgyāṃśānugame sati /
children.translated_text: This group of figures of expressed meaning (<s>vācyālaṅkāra</s>), when accompanied by the suggested element,

children.text: prāyeṇaiva parāṃ chāyāṃ bibhral lakṣye nirīkṣyate // DhvK_3.36 //
children.translated_text: Is almost always seen in [actual] poetic instances (<s>lakṣya</s>) as bearing a surpassing splendor. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 3.36 //

children.text: vācyālaṅkāra-vargo 'yaṃ vyaṅgyāṃśasyālaṅkārasya vastu-mātrasya vā yathā-yogam anugame sati cchāyātiśayaṃ bibhral-lakṣaṇa-kārair eka-deśena darśitaḥ / sa tu tathā-rūpaḥ prāyeṇa sarva eva parīkṣyamāṇo lakṣye nirīkṣyate / tathā hi-dīpaka-samāsoktyādi-vadanye 'py alaṅkārāḥ prāyeṇa vyaṅgyālaṅkārāntara-vastv-antara-saṃsparśino dṛśyante / yataḥ prathamaṃ tāvad atiśayokti-garbhatā sarvālaṅkāreṣu śakya-kriyā / kṛtaiva ca sā mahā-kavibhiḥ kām api kāvyacchaviṃ puṣyati, kathaṃ hy atiśayayogitā sva-viṣayaucityena kriyamāṇā satī kāvye notkarṣam āvahet /
children.translated_text: This group of figures of expressed meaning, when accompanied—as the case may be—by a suggested figure or by mere suggested content, has been shown in part by the makers of definitions as bearing a surpassing splendor. But of that very type, almost all [figures], when examined, are seen in [actual] poetic instances [to bear such splendor]. For instance, the class of <s>dīpaka</s> (illuminator), <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression), and the like—

children.text: bhāmahenāpy atiśayokti-lakṣaṇe yad uktam-
children.translated_text: Even by <s>Bhāmaha</s>, in his definition of <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole), it was said:

children.text:
saiṣā sarvaiva vakroktir anayārtho vibhāvyate /
yatno 'syāṃ kavinā kāryaḥ ko 'laṅkāro 'nayā vinā //iti /
children.translated_text: 'This very <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) is everything; through it, meaning is illuminated. The poet should strive for it—what figure exists without it?'

children.text: tatrātiśayoktir yam alaṅkāram adhitiṣṭhati kavi-pratibhā-vaśāt tasya cārutvātiśaya-yogo 'nyasya tv alaṅkāra-mātrataiveti sarvālaṅkāra-śarīra-svīkaraṇa-yogyatvenābhedopacārāt saiva sarvālaṅkāra-rūpety ayam evārtho 'vagantavyaḥ / tasyāś cālaṅkārāntara-saṃkīrṇatvaṃ kadācid vācyatvena kadacid vyaṅgyatvena / vyaṅgyatvam api kadācit prādhānyena kadācid guṇa-bhāvena / tatrādye pakṣe vācyālaṅkāra-mārgaḥ / dvitīye tu dhvanāv antarbhāvaḥ / tṛtīye tu guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya-rūpatā /
children.translated_text: The <s>atiśayokti</s> [there] refers to that figure upon which it rests through the force of poetic genius (<s>kavi-pratibhā</s>)—its union with a surpassing charm. For another [figure], there is merely the state of being a figure. Through the figurative identification of non-difference (<s>abhedopacāra</s>), since [atiśayokti] is capable of taking on the body of all figures, it alone is said to be the form of all figures—this is the meaning to be understood. And its [identity with each specific] figure—

children.text:
ayaṃ ca prakāro 'nyeṣām apy alaṅkārāṇām asti, teṣāṃ tu na sarva-viṣayaḥ / atiśayoktes tu sarvālaṅkāra-viṣayo 'pi sambhavatīty ayaṃ viśeṣaḥ / yeṣu cālaṅkāreṣu sādṛśya-mukhena tattva-pratilambhaḥ yathā rūpakopamā-tulyayogitā-nidarśanādiṣu teṣu gamyamāna-dharma-mukhenaiva yat sādṛśyaṃ tad eva śobhātiśaya-śāli bhavatīti te sarve 'pi cārutvātiśaya-yoginaḥ santo guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyasyaiva viṣayāḥ / samāsoktyākṣepa-paryāyokty-ādiṣu tu gamyamānāṃśāvinābhāvenaiva tattva-vyavasthānād guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyatā nirvivādaiva /
tatra ca guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyatāyām alaṅkārāṇāṃ keṣāñcid alaṅkāra-viśeṣa-garbhatāyāṃ niyamaḥ / yathā vyāja-stuteḥ preyo 'laṅkāra-garbhatve / keṣāñcid alaṅkāra-mātra-garbhatāyāṃ niyamaḥ / yathā sandehādīnām upamā-garbhatve / keṣāñcid alaṅkārāṇāṃ paraspara-garbhatāpi sambhavati / yathā dīpakopamayoḥ / tatra dīpakam upamā-garbhatvena prasiddham / upamāpi kadācid dīpaka-cchāyānuyāyinī / yathā mālopamā / tathā hi "prabhā-mahatyā śikhayeva dīpaḥ" ity ādau sphuṭaiva dīpaka-cchāyā lakṣyate /
children.translated_text: This variety [of charm-enhancing power] belongs to other figures too, but in their case it does not extend to all [contexts]. The distinction of <s>atiśayokti</s>, however, is that it can extend to all figures. And in those figures where the apprehension of truth comes through the avenue of resemblance—such as <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), <s>upamā</s> (simile), <s>tulya-yogitā</s> (co-predication), <s>nidarśana</s> (illustration), and the like—in them the suggested [element]—

children.text:
tad evaṃ vyaṅgyāṃśa-saṃsparśe sati cārutvātiśaya-yogino rūpakādayo 'laṅkārāḥ sarva eva guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyasya mārgaḥ / guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyatvaṃ ca teṣāṃ tathā-jātīyānāṃ sarveṣām evoktānuktānāṃ sāmānyam / tal-lakṣaṇe sarva evaite sulakṣitā bhavanti / ekaikasya svarūpa-viśeṣa-kathanena tu sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-rahitena pratipāda-pāṭheneva śabdā na śakyante tattvato nirjñātum ānantyāt / anantā hi vāg-vikalpās tat-prakārā eva cālaṅkārāḥ / guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyasya ca prakārāntareṇāpi vyaṅgyārthānugama-lakṣaṇena viṣayatvam asty eva / tad ayaṃ dhvani-niṣyanda-rūpo dvitīyo 'pi mahā-kavi-viṣayo 'tiramaṇīyo lakṣaṇīyaḥ sahṛdayaiḥ /
sarvathā nāsty eva sahṛdaya-hṛdaya-hāriṇaḥ kāvyasya sa prakāro yatra na pratīyamānārtha-saṃsparśena saubhāgyam / tad idaṃ kāvya-rahasyaṃ param iti sūribhir bhāvanīyam /
children.translated_text: Thus, when accompanied by the touch of the suggested element, figures like <s>rūpaka</s> and the rest that possess a surpassing charm are all, without exception, the domain of <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s>. And the state of being <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s> is the general characteristic of all such [figures], both mentioned and unmentioned. Through its definition, all of these are well-characterized. [There is no need] to characterize each one individually—
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 3.37:

children.text: mukhyā mahā-kavi-girām alaṅkṛti-bhṛtām api /
children.translated_text: Of the utterances of great poets, even those adorned with figures—

children.text: pratīyamāna-cchāyaiṣā bhūṣā lajjeva yoṣitām // DhvK_3.37 //
children.translated_text: This splendor of the suggested is their chief ornament, like modesty in women. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 3.37 //

children.text: anayā suprasiddho 'py arthaḥ kim api kāmanīya-kamānīyate / tad yathā-
children.translated_text: By this [suggested splendor], even a well-known meaning is rendered indescribably charming. For example:

children.text: viśrambhotthā manmathājñā-vidhāne
children.translated_text: Those certain special gestures of playfulness (<s>līlā-viśeṣa</s>) of the doe-eyed woman,

children.text: ye mugdhākṣyāḥ ke 'pi līlā-viśeṣāḥ /
children.translated_text: Born of intimacy, in the execution of <s>Manmatha</s>'s (Love's) commands—

children.text: akṣuṇṇās te cetasā kevalena
children.translated_text: Those, inviolate, are to be contemplated continuously with the mind alone,

children.text: sthitvaikānte santataṃ bhāvanīyāḥ //
children.translated_text: While sitting in solitude.

children.text: ity atra ke 'pīty anena padena vācyam aspaṣṭam abhidadhatā pratīyamānaṃ vastv-akliṣṭam anantam arpayatā kā chāyā nopapāditā || DhvA_3.37 ||
children.translated_text: Here, by the word 'certain' (<s>ke 'pi</s>), which renders the expressed meaning indistinct, while offering the suggested content—effortless, boundless—what splendor has not been produced!
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 3.38:

children.text: arthāntara-gatiḥ kākvā yā caiṣā paridṛśyate /
children.translated_text: The apprehension of another meaning through tone of voice (<s>kāku</s>), which is observed—

children.text: sā vyaṅgyasya guṇī-bhāve prakāram imam āśritā // DhvK_3.38 //
children.translated_text: That, when the suggested is subordinate, belongs to this very variety [of <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s>]. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 3.38 //

children.text: yā caiṣā kākvā kvacid arthāntara-pratītirdṛśyate sa vyaṅgyasyārthasya guṇībhāve sati guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya-lakṣaṇaṃ kāvya-prabhedamāśrayate / yathā-"svasthā bhavanti mayi jīvati dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ" / yathā vā-
children.translated_text: The cognition of another meaning through tone of voice (<s>kāku</s>) that is sometimes observed—when the suggested meaning is subordinate, it takes recourse to the variety of poetry defined as <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s>. For example: 'The <s>Dhārtarāṣṭras</s> are well while I am alive.' Or:

children.text: ām asatyaḥ uparama pativrate na tvayā malinitaṃ śīlam /
children.translated_text: 'Oh, you are false! Desist, O faithful wife—your virtue has not been stained by you!

children.text: kiṃ punar janasya jāyeva nāpitaṃ taṃ na kāmayāmahe //
children.translated_text: Why, a woman of the people indeed—we do not desire that barber, do we!'

children.text: śabda-śaktir eva hi svābhidheya-sāmarthyākṣipta-kāku-sahāyā saty artha-viśeṣa-pratipatti-hetur na kāku-mātram / viṣayāntare svecchākṛtāt kāku-mātrāt tathā-vidhārtha-pratipatty-asambhavāt / sa cārthaḥ kāku-viśeṣa-sahāya-śabda-vyāpāropārūḍho 'py artha-sāmarthya-labhya iti vyaṅgya-rūpa eva / vācakatvānugamenaiva tu yadā tad-viśiṣṭa-vācya-pratītis tadā guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyatayā tathā-vidhārtha-dyotinaḥ kāvyasya vyapadeśaḥ / vyaṅgya-viśiṣṭa-vācyābhidhāyino hi guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyatvam /
children.translated_text: For it is the power of words itself—aided by tone of voice (<s>kāku</s>) elicited through the capacity of their own denotation—that is the cause of apprehending the specific meaning, not mere tone of voice alone. Since from mere tone of voice, arbitrarily produced in a different context, such apprehension of meaning would be impossible. And that meaning, though it has mounted upon the verbal function aided by a specific tone of voice, [has the status of suggested]—
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 3.38 [continued]:

children.text: prabhedasyāsya viṣayo yaś ca yuktyā pratīyate /
children.translated_text: And that domain of this variety which is cognized through reasoning (<s>yukti</s>)—

children.text: vidhātavyā sahṛdayair na tatra dhvani-yojanā // DhvK_3.38 //
children.translated_text: There the sensitive reader (<s>sahṛdaya</s>) should not apply the designation '<s>dhvani</s>.' // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 3.38 //

children.text: saṅkīrṇo hi kaścid dhvaner guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyasya ca lakṣye dṛśyate mārgaḥ / tatra yasya yukti-sahāyatā tatra tena vyapadeśaḥ kartavyaḥ / na sarvatra dhvanir āgiṇā bhavitavyam / yathā-
children.translated_text: For a certain mixed path of <s>dhvani</s> and <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s> is observed in [actual] poetic instances. Where reasoning plays a supporting role, the designation should be made accordingly. One should not insist on [the term] '<s>dhvani</s>' everywhere. For example:
