children.translated_text: The apprehension of <s>rasa</s> that arises from contemplating the meaning of this verse is not produced even in the slightest from a meaning expressed straightforwardly as 'Touching you, it sweats, bristles, and trembles.' Thus it has been shown how novelty of poetic meanings arises through recourse to the varieties of <s>dhvani</s>. Through the varieties of <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s> (subordinated suggestion) too — with reference to the suggested [meaning] in its threefold division — novelty of poetic content arises as well. But since that would be too expansive, it has not been illustrated; the sensitive reader should imagine it on his own. [End of <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.5]
[<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.6:]

children.text: dhvaner itthaṃ guṇībhūta-vyaṅgyasya ca samāśrayāt /
children.translated_text: Through recourse to <s>dhvani</s> and to <s>guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya</s> (subordinated suggestion) thus,

children.text: na kāvyārtha-virāmo 'sti yadi syāt pratibhā-guṇaḥ // DhvK_4.6 //
children.translated_text: There is no end to poetic meanings — provided the quality of creative genius (<s>pratibhā</s>) exists. [End of <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.6]

children.text: satsv api purātana-kavi-prabandheṣu yadi syāt pratibhā-guṇaḥ, tasmiṃs tv asati na kiṃcid eva kaver vastv asti / bandha-cchāyāpy artha-dvayānurūpa-śabda-sanniveśo 'rtha-pratibhānābhāve katham upapadyate / anapekṣitārtha-viśeṣākṣara-racanaiva bandha-cchāyeti nedaṃ nedīyaḥ sahṛdayānām / evaṃ hi saty arthānapekṣa-catura-madhura-vacana-racanāyām api kāvya-vyapadeśaḥ pravarteta / śabdārthayoḥ sāhityena kāvyatve kathaṃ tathā-vidhe viṣaye kāvya-vyavastheti cet-paropanibaddhārtha-viracane yathā tat-kāvyatva-vyavahāras tathā tathā-vidhānāṃ kāvya-sandarbhāṇām || DhvA_4.6 ||
children.translated_text: Even though the compositions of ancient poets already exist, if the quality of creative genius is present [in a new poet, novelty arises]; but in its absence, the poet has nothing whatsoever. And the quality of composition (<s>bandha-chāyā</s>) — the arrangement of words conformable to both [expressed and suggested] meanings — how can it be achieved without the flash of meaning? 'The mere arrangement of letters without regard to particular meaning is the quality of composition' — this is far from [the understanding of] the sensitive. For if it were so, even in the composition of clever and sweet utterances irrespective of meaning, the designation 'poetry' would apply. If asked, 'Since poetry consists in the union of word and meaning, how can the designation of poetry apply in such a case?' — [the answer is:] just as the practice of calling [something] poetry applies to [works] composed with meaning borrowed from others, so it is with such poetic compositions. [End of <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.6]

children.text: na cārthānantyaṃ vyaṅgyārthāpekṣayaiva yāvad vācyārthāpekṣayāpīti pratipādayitum ucyate-
children.translated_text: And to establish that infinity [of meaning] exists not only with reference to suggested meaning but also with reference to expressed meaning, it is said:
[<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.7:]

children.text: avasthādeśa-kālādi-viśeṣair api jāyate /
children.translated_text: Through distinctions of state, place, time, and the like,

children.text: ānantyam eva vācyasya śuddhasyāpi svabhāvataḥ // DhvK_4.7 //
children.translated_text: Infinity arises even for the purely expressed meaning, by its very nature. [End of <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.7]

children.text: śuddhasyānapekṣita-vyaṅgyasyāpi vācyasyānantyam eva jāyate svabhāvataḥ / svabhāvo hy ayaṃ vācyānāṃ cetanānām acetanānāṃ ca yad avasthā-bhedād deśa-bhedāt kāla-bhedāt svālakṣaṇya-bhedāc cānantatā bhavati / taiś ca tathā-vyavasthitaiḥ sadbhiḥ prasiddhāneka-svabhāvānusaraṇa-rūpayā svabhāvoktyāpi tāvad upanibadhyamānair niravadhiḥ kāvyārthaḥ sampadyate /
children.translated_text: Even for the expressed meaning that is purely [expressed], without regard to the suggested, infinity arises by nature. For it is the nature of expressed [objects] — both sentient and insentient — that through distinctions of state, place, time, and individual characteristics, they are infinite. And when these, being so constituted, are composed through <s>svabhāvokti</s> (natural description) — which consists in following their manifold well-known natures — even then, boundless poetic meaning results.

children.text: tathā hy avasthā-bhedān navatvaṃ yathā-bhagavatī pārvatī kumārasambhave "sarvopamā-dravya-samuccayena" [ku.saṃ. 1.49] ity ādibhir uktibhiḥ prathamam eva parisamāpita-rūpa-varṇanāpi punar bhagavataḥ śambhor locana-gocaram āyāntī "vasanta-puṣpābharaṇaṃ vahantī" [ku.saṃ. 3.53] manmathopakaraṇa-bhūtena bhaṅgyantareṇopavarṇitā / saiva ca punar navodvāha-samaye prasādhyamānā "tāṃ prāṅ-mukhīṃ tatra niveśya tanvīm" ity ādy-uktibhir navenaiva prakāreṇa nirūpita-rūpa-sauṣṭhavā /
children.translated_text: For example, novelty through distinction of states: The divine <s>Pārvatī</s> in the <s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s>, though her beauty has been completely described at the very outset through utterances such as 'with an assemblage of all objects of comparison' [<s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s> 1.49] and the like — is described yet again, when she comes within the sight of Lord <s>Śambhu</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), through a different turn of phrase, as one 'bearing the ornament of spring-flowers' [<s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s> 3.53], serving as an instrument of <s>Kāma</s> (Love). And that very [<s>Pārvatī</s>] is again, at the time of the wedding, as she is being adorned — described in yet another novel manner through utterances such as 'Having seated that slender one facing east' and the like, with her beauty of form portrayed in a new way.

children.text: na ca te tasya kaver ekatraivāsakṛt-kṛtā varṇana-prakārā apunar-uktatvena vā nava-navārtha-nirbharatvena vā pratibhāsante / darśitam eva caitad viṣama-bāṇa-līlāyām-
children.translated_text: Nor do those modes of description, employed by that poet more than once in a single [work], appear as repetitious — rather, they appear as brimming with ever-new meanings. And this was shown in the <s>Viṣamabāṇalīlā</s>:

children.text: ṇa a tāṇaṃ ghaḍa(i) ohī ṇa a te dīsanti kaha bi punaruttā /
children.translated_text: Neither does a limit form for them, nor do they ever appear as repetition —

children.text: je bibbhamā piāṇaṃ atthā vā suka(i)-bāṇīnaṃ //
children.translated_text: The amorous gestures of beloveds, or the meanings of good poets' words.

children.text: [na ca teṣāṃ ghaṭate 'vadhiḥ, na ca te dṛśyante katham api punaruktāḥ /
children.translated_text: [Neither does a limit form for them, nor do they ever appear as repetition —

children.text: ye vibhramāḥ priyāṇām arthā vā sukavi-vāṇīnām //]
children.translated_text: The amorous gestures of beloveds, or the meanings of good poets' words.]

children.text: ayam aparaś cāvasthā-bheda-prakāro yad acetanānāṃ sarveṣāṃ cetanaṃ dvitīyaṃ rūpam abhimānitva-prasiddhaṃ himavad gaṅgādīnām / tac cocita-cetana-viṣaya-svarūpa-yojanayopanibadhyamānam anyad eva sampadyate / yathā kumāra-sambhava eva parvata-svarūpasya himavato varṇanaṃ, punaḥ saptarṣi-priyoktiṣu cetana-tat-svarūpāpekṣayā pradarśitaṃ tad apūrvam eva pratibhāti / prasiddhaś cāyaṃ sat-kavīnāṃ mārgaḥ / idaṃ ca prasthānaṃ kavi-vyutpattaye viṣama-bāṇa-līlāyāṃ sa-prapañcaṃ darśitam / cetanānāṃ ca bālyādy-avasthābhir anyatvaṃ sat-kavīnāṃ prasiddham eva / cetanānām avasthā-bhede 'py avāntarāvasthā-bhedān nānātvam / yathā kumārīṇāṃ kusuma-śara-bhinna-hṛdayānām anyāsāṃ ca / tatrāpi vinītānām avinītānāṃ ca / acetanānāṃ ca bhāvānām ārambhādy-avasthā-bheda-bhinnānām ekaikaśaḥ svarūpam upanibadhyamānam ānantyam evopayāti / yathā-
children.translated_text: And here is another mode [of novelty] through distinction of states: all inanimate objects have a second, sentient nature that is attributed [to them by convention] — as is well known for <s>Himavat</s> (the Himālaya), the <s>Gaṅgā</s>, and the like. And when that [sentient nature] is composed by fitting an appropriate sentient character to [the object's] form, [the description] becomes something entirely different. As in the <s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s> itself: the description of <s>Himavat</s>'s mountain-nature [in the first canto] is presented again in the loving words of the Seven Sages with reference to his sentient nature — and that appears as entirely novel. And this is a well-known path of good poets. This approach has been shown with full elaboration in the <s>Viṣamabāṇalīlā</s> for the training of poets. And for sentient beings, novelty through the stages of childhood etc. is well known among good poets. Even within distinctions of state, further sub-distinctions [produce] multiplicity — as for maidens whose hearts have been pierced by the arrows of <s>Kāma</s> (Love), versus others; and among those, the modest versus the immodest. And for inanimate states as well — differentiated by stages such as inception etc. — each one's nature, when composed individually, approaches infinity. As in:

children.text: haṃsānāṃ ninadeṣu yaiḥ kavalitair āsajyate kūjatām
children.translated_text: Those [filaments] that, when swallowed by the geese in the midst of their calls,

children.text: anyaḥ ko 'pi kaṣāya-kaṇṭha-luṭhanād āghargharo vibhramaḥ /
children.translated_text: Produce some other indescribable, delightful tremor from the gargling of their bitter throats —

children.text: te sampraty akaṭhora-vāraṇa-vadhū-dantāṅkura-spardhino
children.translated_text: Those [filaments] now rival the tender tusk-buds of young elephant-cows,

children.text: niryātāḥ kamalākareṣu bisinī-kandāgrima-granthayaḥ //[*23]
children.translated_text: [Having] emerged in the lotus-ponds — the first knotted joints of lotus-root fibers.
Reference: Srk 284, Skm 1309 (credited to <s>Kamalāyudha</s>)

children.text: Srk 284, Skm 1309 (credited to Kamalāyudha)

evam anyatrāpi diśānayānusartavyam / deśa-bhedān nānātvam acetanānāṃ tāvat / yathā vāyūnāṃ nānā-dig-deśa-cāriṇām anyeṣām api salila-kusumādīnāṃ prasiddham eva / cetanānām api mānuṣa-paśu-pakṣi-prabhṛtīnāṃ grāmāraṇya-salilādi-samedhitānāṃ parasparaṃ mahān viśeṣaḥ samupalakṣyata eva / sa ca vivicya yathāyatham upanibadhyamānas tathaivānantyam āyāti / tathā hi-mānuṣāṇām eva tāvad dig-deśādi-bhinnānāṃ ye vyavahāra-vyāpārādiṣu vicitrā viśeṣās teṣāṃ kenāntaḥ śakyate gantum, viśeṣato yoṣitām / upanibadhyate ca tat sarvam eva sukavibhir yathā-pratibham /
children.translated_text: In the same way, elsewhere too, this method should be followed. Diversity arising from difference of region (<s>deśa-bheda</s>)—first, of inanimate things: as with winds blowing in various directions, and of others such as water, flowers, and so on, [diversity] is well-known. Of sentient beings too—humans, animals, birds, and the rest, nourished by village, forest, water, and the like—a great distinction among them is indeed observed. And that [distinction], when discriminated—

children.text: kāla-bhedāc ca nānātvam / yatha rtu-bhedād dig-vyoma-salilādīnām acetanānām / cetanānāṃ cautsukyādayaḥ kāla-viśeṣāśrayiṇaḥ prasiddhā eva / svālakṣaṇya-prabhedāc ca sakala-jagad-gatānāṃ vastūnāṃ vinibandhanaṃ prasiddham eva / tac ca yathāvasthitam api tāvad upanibadhyamānam anantatām eva kāvyārthasyāpādayati /
children.translated_text: And diversity arising from difference of time (<s>kāla-bheda</s>): as with inanimate things like the quarters, sky, waters, and so on [varying] with the seasons. Of sentient beings too, eagerness (<s>autsukyā</s>) and the like, which depend on particular times, are well-known. And the poetic binding of all things in the world according to their individual uniqueness (<s>svālakṣaṇya</s>) is well-established. And even that, being composed just as it actually is, endows the content of poetry with endlessness—

children.text: atra kecid ācakṣīran-yathā sāmānyātmanā vastūni vācyatāṃ pratipadyante na viśeṣātmanā ; tāni hi svayam anubhūtānāṃ sukhādīnāṃ tan-nimittānāṃ ca svarūpam anyatrāropayadbhiḥ sva-parānubhūta-rūpa-sāmānya-mātrāśrayeṇopanibadhyante kavibhiḥ / na hi tair atītam anāgataṃ vartamānaṃ ca paricitādi-sva-lakṣaṇaṃ yogibhir iva pratyakṣīkriyate ; tac cānubhāvyānubhava-sāmānyaṃ sarva-pratipattṛ-sādhāraṇaṃ parimitatvāt purātanānām eva gocarī-bhūtam, tasyāviṣayatvānupapatteḥ / ata eva sa prakāra-viśeṣo yair adyatanair abhinavatvena pratīyate teṣām abhimāna-mātram eva bhaṇiti-kṛtaṃ vaicitrya-mātram atrāstīti /
children.translated_text: Here some might say: just as things enter into the status of being expressed in their generic aspect (<s>sāmānya</s>) and not in their particular aspect (<s>viśeṣa</s>)—for they are composed by poets who project the nature of pleasures and the like, experienced by themselves, and their causes, onto other [subjects], relying merely on the generic form of what has been experienced by self and others. For by those [poets], the past, future, and present, with their individual characteristics familiar and unfamiliar—

children.text: tatrocyate-yat tūktaṃ sāmānya-mātrāśrayeṇa kāvya-pravṛttis tasya ca parimitatvena prāg eva gocarī-kṛtatvān nāsti navatvaṃ kāvya-vastūnām iti, tad ayuktam ; yato yadi sāmānya-mātram āśritya kāvyaṃ pravartate kiṃ kṛtas tarhi mahā-kavi-nibadhyamānānāṃ kāvyārthānām atiśayaḥ / vālmīki-vyatiriktasyānyasya kavi-vyapadeśa eva vā sāmānya-vyatiriktasyānyasya kāvyārthasyābhāvāt, sāmānyasya cādikavinaiva pradarśitatvāt / ukti-vaicitryān naiṣa doṣa iti cet-kim idam ukti-vaicitryam ? uktir hi vācya-viśeṣa-pratipādi vacanam / tad-vaicitrye kathaṃ na vācya-vaicitryam ? vācya-vācakayor avinābhāvena pravṛtteḥ / vācyānāṃ ca kāvye pratibhāsamānānāṃ yad rūpaṃ tat tu grāhya-viśeṣābhedenaiva pratīyate / tenokti-vaicitrya-vādinā vācya-vaicitryam anicchatāpy avaśyam evābhyupagantavyam / tad ayam atra saṅkṣepaḥ-
children.translated_text: To this we reply: the assertion that poetic activity relies merely on the generic, and that since the generic is limited and has been exhausted long ago, there is no novelty in poetic subjects—that is incorrect. For if poetry operates relying merely on the generic, then why is there the surpassing excellence of poetic contents composed by great poets? If for anyone other than <s>Vālmīki</s>—

children.text: vālmīki-vyatiriktasya yady ekasyāpi kasyacit /
children.translated_text: If for even one other than <s>Vālmīki</s>,

children.text: iṣyate pratibhārtheṣu tat tad ānantyam akṣayam //
children.translated_text: Genius in poetic subjects is acknowledged—that endlessness [of poetry] is inexhaustible.

children.text: kiṃ ca, ukti-vaicitryaṃ yat kāvya-navatve nibandhanam ucyate tad asmat-pakṣānuguṇam eva / yato yāvān ayaṃ kāvyārthānantya-bheda-hetuḥ prakāraḥ prāg darśitaḥ sa sarva eva punarukti-vaicitryād dvi-guṇatām āpadyate / yaś cāyam upamā-śleṣādir alaṅkāra-vargaḥ prasiddhaḥ sa bhaṇiti-vaicitryād upanibadhyamānaḥ svayam evānavadhir dhatte punaḥ śata-śākhatām / bhaṇitiś ca sva-bhāṣā-bhedena vyavasthitā satī pratiniyata-bhāṣā-gocarārtha-vaicitrya-nibandhanaṃ punar aparaṃ kāvyārthānām ānantyam āpādayati / yathā mamaiva-
children.translated_text: Moreover, what is called 'variety of expression' (<s>ukti-vaicitrya</s>), said to be the basis of novelty in poetry, actually supports our position. For the entire range of causes of the infinite variety of poetic content demonstrated earlier is doubled through variety of expression. And the well-known group of figures such as simile (<s>upamā</s>), paronomasia (<s>śleṣa</s>), and the like, when composed with variety of diction—

children.text: maha maha iti bhaṇantaho bajjadi kālo jaṇassa /
children.translated_text: 'Mine, mine!'—so saying, the time of people passes;

children.text: toi ṇa deu janaddaṇu goarībhodi maṇassa //
children.translated_text: Yet even so, Lord <s>Janārdana</s> does not come within the reach of the mind.

children.text: [mama mama iti bhaṇato vrajati kālo janasya /
children.translated_text: ['Mine, mine!'—so saying, the time of people passes;

children.text: tathāpi na devo janārdano gocaro bhavati manasaḥ] || DhvA_4.7 ||
children.translated_text: Yet even so, Lord <s>Janārdana</s> does not come within the reach of the mind.]

children.text: itthaṃ yathā yathā nirūpyate tathā tathā na labhyate 'ntaḥ kāvyārthānām / idaṃ tūcyate-
children.translated_text: Thus, the more one examines, the more one cannot find an end to poetic subjects. But this is said:
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.8:

children.text:
avasthādi-vibhinnānāṃ vācyānāṃ vinibandhanam /
yat pradarśitaṃ prāk-
children.translated_text: The composition of expressible contents differentiated by condition (<s>avasthā</s>) and the like, which was demonstrated earlier—

children.text: bhūmnaiva dṛśyate lakṣye . . . . . . . . . . .
children.translated_text: Is seen overwhelmingly in [actual] poetic instances (<s>lakṣya</s>) . . .

children.text: na tac chakyam apohitum /
children.translated_text: That cannot be set aside;

children.text: . . . . . . . . . . .tat tu bhāti rasāśrayāt // DhvK_4.8 //
children.translated_text: . . . but it shines through its grounding in <s>rasa</s>. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.8 //

children.text: tad idam atra saṅkṣepeṇābhidhīyate sat-kavīnām upadeśāya-
children.translated_text: This is stated here in summary, as instruction for good poets:
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.9:

children.text: rasa-bhāvādi-sambaddhā yady aucityānusāriṇī /
children.translated_text: If the course of subject-matter (<s>vastu-gati</s>), differentiated by region, time, and the like,

children.text: anvīyate vastu-gatir deśa-kālādi-bhedinī // DhvK_4.9 //
children.translated_text: Is pursued in conformity with propriety (<s>aucitya</s>) and connected with <s>rasa</s> and <s>bhāva</s>— // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.9 //

children.text: tatkā gaṇanā kavīnāmanyeṣāṃ parimitaśaktīnām /
children.translated_text: Then what reckoning can there be of other poets of limited power?
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.10:

children.text: vācaspati-sahasrāṇāṃ sahasrair api yatnataḥ /
children.translated_text: Even by thousands of <s>Vācaspatis</s> (lords of speech), with thousands of efforts,

children.text: nibaddhā sā kṣayaṃ naiti prakṛtir jagatām iva // DhvK_4.10 //
children.translated_text: That [poetic nature], once composed, does not reach exhaustion—like the nature of the world itself. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.10 //

children.text: yathā hi jagat-prakṛtir atīta-kalpa-paramparāvirbhūta-vicitra-vastu-prapañcā satī punar idānīṃ parikṣīṇā para-padārtha-nirmāṇa-śaktir iti na śakyate 'bhidhātum / tadvad eveyaṃ kāvya-sthitir anantābhiḥ kavi-matibhir upabhuktāpi nedānīṃ parihīyate, pratyuta nava-navābhir vyutpattibhiḥ parivardhate / itthaṃ sthite 'pi
children.translated_text: For just as the nature of the world (<s>jagat-prakṛti</s>), though it has manifested the varied expanse of things through an unbroken succession of past world-cycles (<s>kalpa</s>), cannot be said to have now exhausted its power to create further entities—in the very same way, this state of poetry, though partaken of by countless poetic minds, is not diminished now; rather, it grows ever greater through ever-new cultivations of learning. Thus—
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.11:

children.text: saṃvādās tu bhavanty eva bāhulyena sumedhasām /
children.translated_text: Concordances (<s>saṃvāda</s>) do indeed occur abundantly among persons of keen intellect;

children.text: sthitaṃ hy etat saṃvādinya eva medhāvināṃ buddhayaḥ /
children.translated_text: For it is established that the intellects of the wise do indeed correspond [with one another].

children.text: kintu-
children.translated_text: However—

children.text: naika-rūpatayā sarve te mantavyā vipaścitā // DhvK_4.11 //
children.translated_text: They should not all be regarded as of one form by the discerning. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.11 //

children.text: katham iti cet-
children.translated_text: How so?
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.12:

children.text: saṃvādo hy anya-sādṛśyaṃ tat punaḥ pratibimbavat /
children.translated_text: For concordance is resemblance to another; and that [resemblance] is like a reflection,

children.text: ālekhyākāravat tulya-dehivac ca śarīriṇām // DhvK_4.12 //
children.translated_text: Like the form in a painting, and like one having an identical body—[these are the three types] among embodied beings. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.12 //

children.text: saṃvādo hi kāvyārthasyocyate yad anyena kāvya-vastunā sādṛśyam / tat punaḥ śarīriṇāṃ pratibimbavad ālekhyākāravat tulya-dehivac ca tridhā vyavasthitam / kiṃcid dhi kāvya-vastu vastv-antarasya śarīriṇaḥ pratibimba-kalpam, anyad ālekhya-prakhyam, anyat tulyena śarīriṇā sadṛśam /
children.translated_text: Concordance (<s>saṃvāda</s>) in poetic content is said to be resemblance to another poetic subject. That [resemblance] is established in three ways among embodied beings: like a reflection (<s>pratibimba</s>), like a painted likeness (<s>ālekhya</s>), and like one having an identical body (<s>tulya-dehin</s>). For some poetic subject is like the reflection of another embodied subject; another is like a painting; and yet another resembles [the other] as one having an identical body.
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.13:

children.text: tatra pūrvam ananyātma tucchātma tad-anantaram /
children.translated_text: Of these, the first has no independent essence; the second has an insubstantial essence;

children.text: tṛtīyaṃ tu prasiddhātma nānya-sāmyaṃ tyajet kaviḥ // DhvK_4.13 //
children.translated_text: But the third has a well-established essence—the poet should not abandon resemblance to another [of this third kind]. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.13 //

children.text: tatra pūrvaṃ pratibimba-kalpaṃ kāvya-vastu parihartavyaṃ sumatinā / yatas tad-ananyātma tāttvika-śarīra-śūnyam / tad-anantaram ālekhya-prakhyam anya-sāmyaṃ śarīrāntara-yuktam api tucchātmatvena tyaktavyam / tṛtīyaṃ tu vibhinna-kamanīya-śarīra-sadbhāve sati sasaṃvādam api kāvya-vastu na tyaktavyaṃ kavinā / na hi śarīrī śarīriṇānyena sadṛśo 'py eka eveti śakyate vaktum || DhvA_4.13 ||
children.translated_text: Of these, the first—poetic content like a reflection—should be avoided by the wise, since it has no independent essence and is devoid of a true body. The second—resemblance to another like a painting—even though it possesses another body, should be abandoned because of its insubstantial nature. But the third—when there exists a distinct and charming body [of its own]—even though it has concordance [with another], such poetic content should not be abandoned by the poet—

children.text: etad evopapādayitum ucyate-
children.translated_text: To establish this very point, it is said:
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.14:

children.text: ātmano 'nyasya sad-bhāve pūrva-sthity-anuyāyy api /
children.translated_text: When the essential nature [is independently] present, even a subject that follows a prior [composition]

children.text: vastu bhātitarāṃ tanvyāḥ śaśi-cchāyam ivānanam // DhvK_4.14 //
children.translated_text: Shines all the more—like the face of a slender woman [that shines more] with the splendor of the moon [reflected in it]. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.14 //

children.text:
tattvasya sāra-bhūtasyātmanaḥ sad-bhāve 'nyasya pūrva-sthity-anuyāyy api vastu bhātitarām /
purāṇa-ramaṇīya-cchāyānugṛhītaṃ hi vastu śarīravat parāṃ śobhāṃ puṣyati / na tu punar-uktatvenāvabhāsate / tanvyāḥ śaśi-cchāyam ivānanam || DhvA_4.14 ||
children.translated_text: When the essential core (<s>sāra-bhūta ātman</s>) is present, even a subject that follows a prior [composition] shines all the more. For a subject graced by a charming ancient splendor flourishes in supreme beauty, like a body [adorned]. It does not appear as mere repetition. Like the face of a slender woman with the splendor of the moon [reflected in it].

children.text: evaṃ tāvat sa-saṃvādānāṃ samudāya-rūpāṇāṃ vākyārthānāṃ vibhaktāḥ sīmānaḥ / padārtha-rūpāṇāṃ ca vastv-antara-sadṛśānāṃ kāvya-vastūnāṃ nāsty eva doṣa iti pratipādayitum ucyate-
children.translated_text: Thus far, the boundaries of concordant poetic sentence-meanings in their collective form have been distinguished. To demonstrate that in the case of poetic subjects of the word-meaning type that resemble other subjects, there is no fault at all, it is said:
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.15:

children.text: akṣarādi-racaneva yojyate yatra vastu-racanā purātanī /
children.translated_text: Where the arrangement of subject-matter is ancient, like the arrangement of syllables and the like,

children.text: nūtane sphurati kāvya-vastuni vyaktam eva khalu sā na duṣyati // DhvK_4.15 //
children.translated_text: When it shines forth in a new poetic subject, it clearly does not become faulty. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.15 //

children.text: na hi vācaspatināpy akṣarāṇi padāni vā kānicid apūrvāṇi ghaṭayituṃ śakyante / tāni tu tāny evopanibaddhāni na kāvyādiṣu navatāṃ virudhyanti / tathaiva padārtha-rūpāṇi śleṣādi-mayāny artha-tattvāni / tasmāt-
children.translated_text: For not even <s>Vācaspati</s> (<s>Bṛhaspati</s>) himself could fashion any wholly unprecedented syllables or words. Yet those very [syllables and words], when composed [anew], do not obstruct novelty in poetry and the like. In the same way, word-meaning-level truths of meaning, consisting of paronomasia (<s>śleṣa</s>) and the like, [do not obstruct novelty]. Therefore:
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.16:

children.text: yadapi tad api ramyaṃ . . . . . . . .
children.translated_text: Even that is charming . . .

children.text:
kāvya-śarīraṃ
. . . . . . . . yatra lokasya kiṃcit
children.translated_text: The body of poetry . . . where something of the world—

children.text: yal lokasya kiṃcit /
children.translated_text: Something of the world—

children.text: sphuritam idam itīyaṃ buddhir abhyujjihīte /
children.translated_text: 'This has flashed forth here!'—this cognition arises;

children.text: sphuraṇeyaṃ kācid iti sahṛdayānāṃ camatkṛtir utpadyate /
children.translated_text: 'What a flash this is!'—thus arises the wonder (<s>camatkṛti</s>) of sensitive readers (<s>sahṛdaya</s>).

children.text: anugatam api pūrva-cchāyayā vastu tādṛk
sukavir upanibadhnan nindyatāṃ nopayāti // DhvK_4.16 //
children.translated_text: A good poet composing it does not incur blame. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.16 //
Even a subject accompanied by the splendor of a prior [composition], such [a subject]—

children.text: tad-anugatam api pūrva-cchāyayā vastu tādṛk tādṛkṣaṃ sukavir vivakṣita-vyaṅgya-vācyārtha-samarpaṇa-samartha-śabda-racanā-rūpayā bandha-cchāyayopanibadhnan-nindyatāṃ naiva yāti / tad itthaṃ sthitam-
children.translated_text: Even a subject accompanied by the splendor of a prior [composition], such a subject—a good poet composing it with the splendor of composition (<s>bandha-cchāyā</s>), in the form of a verbal arrangement capable of presenting the intended suggested and expressed meanings—does not at all incur blame. Thus it is established:
<s>Dhvanyāloka</s> 4.17:

children.text:
pratīyantāṃ vāco nimita-vividhārthāmṛta-rasā
na sādaḥ kartavyaḥ kavibhir anavadye sva-viṣaye /
children.translated_text: Let utterances be produced, steeped in the nectar of manifold meanings; let poets not lose heart in their own blameless domain.

children.text: santi navāḥ kāvyārthāḥ paropanibaddhārtha-viracane na kaścit kaver guṇa iti bhāvayitvā /
children.translated_text: Thinking 'there are no new poetic subjects; there is no merit for a poet in composing what has been composed by others'—

children.text: parasvādānecchā-virata-manaso vastu sukaveḥ
sarasvaty evaiṣā ghaṭayati yatheṣṭaṃ bhagavatī // DhvK_4.17 //
children.translated_text: The blessed goddess <s>Sarasvatī</s> herself fashions subject-matter as she pleases. // <s>Dhvanyāloka</s> Kārikā 4.17 //
For the good poet whose mind has ceased from the desire to taste what belongs to others,

children.text: para-svādānecchāvirata-manasaḥ sukaveḥ sarasvaty eṣā bhagavatī yatheṣṭaṃ ghaṭayati vastu / yeṣāṃ sukavīnāṃ prāktana-puṇyābhyāsa-paripāka-vaśena pravṛttis teṣāṃ paroparacitārtha-parigraha-niḥspṛhāṇāṃ sva-vyāpāro na kvacid upayujyate / saiva bhagavatī sarasvatī svayam abhimatam artham āvirbhāvayati / etad eva hi mahākavitvaṃ mahākavīnām ity om /
children.translated_text: For the good poet whose mind has withdrawn from the desire to taste what belongs to others, the blessed goddess <s>Sarasvatī</s> fashions subject-matter as she pleases. For those good poets whose creative activity proceeds from the maturation of merit accumulated in former lives, and who are free from the desire to appropriate content fashioned by others—their own effort is nowhere needed. The blessed <s>Sarasvatī</s> herself brings forth the desired content.

children.text: ity akliṣṭa-rasāśrayocita-guṇālaṅkāra-śobhā-bhṛto
children.translated_text: Since all the desired subject-matter, bearing the splendor of qualities (<s>guṇa</s>) and figures (<s>alaṅkāra</s>) appropriate to effortless <s>rasa</s>,

children.text: yasmād vastu samīhitaṃ sukṛtibhiḥ sarvaṃ samāsādyate /
children.translated_text: Is attained by the meritorious—

children.text: kāvyākhye 'khila-saukhya-dhāmni vibudhodyāne dhvanir darśitaḥ
children.translated_text: In that divine garden of poetry, the abode of all delight, this <s>dhvani</s> has been shown,

children.text: so 'yaṃ kalpatarūpamāna-mahimā bhogyo 'stu bhavyātmanām //
children.translated_text: Whose glory equals that of the wish-fulfilling tree (<s>kalpataru</s>)—may it be enjoyed by those of noble nature!

children.text: sat-kāvya-tattva-naya-vartma-cira-prasupta-
children.translated_text: That path to the true nature of good poetry—which had long been asleep, as it were,

children.text: kalpaṃ manaḥsu paripakva-dhiyāṃ yadāsīt /
children.translated_text: In the minds of those of ripened intellect—

children.text: tad vyākarot sahṛdayodaya-lābha-hetor
children.translated_text: That was illuminated, for the sake of evoking the delight of sensitive readers (<s>sahṛdaya</s>),

children.text: ānandavardhana iti prathitābhidhānaḥ //
children.translated_text: By the one renowned by the name <s>Ānandavardhana</s>.

children.text: iti śrī-rājānakānanda-vardhanācārya-viracite dhvany-āloke caturtha uddyotaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus ends the Fourth <s>Uddyota</s> (Illumination) of the <s>Dhvanyāloka</s>, composed by the revered master <s>Rājānaka Ānandavardhana</s>.
